messages.kimi:
[build] Enable Flash Attention for ROCm/HIP backend (#156XXX)

Add Flash Attention support for AMD GPUs (MI200/MI250, gfx90a) by introducing
HIP-specific implementation files and updating CMake configuration to build
flash attention kernels on ROCm platform.

Key changes:
- Add new flash attention HIP source files (flash_api.hip) implementing
  mha_fwd, mha_bwd, and mha_varlen_fwd for ROCm
- Update CMakeLists.txt to conditionally enable USE_FLASH_ATTENTION for
  ROCm (not just CUDA) and include composable_kernel headers
- Modify sdp_utils.cpp to add gfx90a hardware support check with
  PYTORCH_DEBUG_FLASH_ATTENTION_GCN_ARCH_OVERRIDE for testing
- Update attention.cpp to route HIP dispatch keys to fused SDPA path
- Add ROCm-specific test skips and PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_FLASH_ATTENTION
  evaluation for gfx90a architecture

This enables flash attention acceleration on AMD MI200/MI250 GPUs, matching
the CUDA implementation's functionality while respecting ROCm's specific
hardware constraints (gfx90a only, fp16/bf16 support).
messages.claude:
[feat] Enable ROCm flash attention backend for SDPA

Add ROCm/HIP support for the flash attention scaled dot product attention
backend, building on the existing CUDA implementation.

What:
- Introduce a CONFIG_FA gate in the top-level CMakeLists.txt that enables
  USE_FLASH_ATTENTION for ROCm builds (in addition to the existing CUDA path),
  with a TODO to consolidate into cmake_dependent_option once
  cmake_minimum_required is bumped to 3.22 (CMP0127).
- Wire flash attention HIP sources into aten/src/ATen/CMakeLists.txt, including
  the new composable_kernel include paths and the OORT-based hip kernels.
- Route _fused_sdp_choice and scaled_dot_product_attention through the HIP
  dispatch key when USE_ROCM is defined, so the fused backend is selected on
  AMD GPUs instead of falling back to math.
- Add a gfx90a (MI200/MI250) hardware support check in sdp_utils.cpp guarded
  by USE_ROCM, with a PYTORCH_DEBUG_FLASH_ATTENTION_GCN_ARCH_OVERRIDE escape
  hatch for testing on non-gfx90a parts.
- Add the new flash_api.hip implementation (forward/backward wrappers around the
  OORT kernels) plus the supporting ck/tile programming headers under
  aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/hip/flash_attn.
- Update tools/amd_build/build_amd.py to hipify only the specific transformers
  CUDA files that are shared, rather than the whole directory.
- Add CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING -> AMD_SERIALIZE_KERNEL mappings to hipify.
- Adjust tests: gate PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_FLASH_ATTENTION on gfx90a for ROCm,
  skip nested-tensor and lower-right causal variant cases that the ROCm backend
  does not yet support.

Why:
ROCm users had no fused flash attention path and were forced onto the math
backend for scaled_dot_product_attention, leaving significant performance on
the table for MI200/MI250 GPUs. The OORT/composable_kernel-based implementation
exposed here provides a native HIP flash attention kernel that plugs into the
existing SDPA dispatcher, closing the performance gap with the CUDA backend
while keeping the CUDA path unchanged. The arch override and test skips keep CI
honest about current limitations (only gfx90a supported, no nested tensor or
lower-right causal variant yet) without blocking the rest of the ROCm test
suite.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/98214
Approved by: https://github.com/ngimel, https://github.com/Drizin

messages.kimi:
fix: Preserve state_dict identity in ExportedProgram after decomposition

Summary: Remove unnecessary state_dict copy in ExportedProgram's decomposition method to preserve state_dict identity across transformations.

Reason: The previous implementation created a shallow copy of state_dict during decomposition, causing `ep.state_dict` to return a different object after calling `run_decompositions()`. This broke user expectations that the state_dict reference should remain stable, as demonstrated by the test asserting `id(state_dict) == id(ep.state_dict)`. By passing `self.state_dict` directly instead of a copy, we maintain object identity while still achieving correct behavior since the state_dict is not modified in place.
messages.minimax:
fix export preserve state_dict identity instead of creating copy

The ExportedProgram was creating a copy of state_dict during transforms, which broke identity checks in downstream code that relied on `ep.state_dict` being the same object. Changed to pass `self.state_dict` directly to preserve the reference. Added test assertion to verify state_dict identity is maintained through the export process.
messages.claude:
fix: preserve state_dict identity in ExportedProgram.transform

The transform() method was creating a copy of state_dict via
`state_dict = self.state_dict.copy()` and passing the copy into the new
ExportedProgram. This broke object identity: callers who held a
reference to the original program's state_dict would see a different
object after transform, and mutations to one would not be reflected in
the other.

This matters for workflows where the same state_dict is shared across
the original and transformed programs (e.g. after
`run_decompositions`), since copy-on-transform silently desynced them.

Pass `self.state_dict` directly so the transformed program aliases the
same dict. Added a test asserting `id(state_dict) ==
id(ep.state_dict)` after decomposition to guard against regression.

[ez] include config as part of __all__ in torch.compiler (#148978)

Right now we are susceptive to a race condition where if the torch.compiler.config is not implicitly import via dynamo/builder.py, we will throw an error when trying to set compiler configs. This fixes it by including config in `__all__`.

```
>>> import torch

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: module 'torch.compiler' has no attribute 'config'

"L['kwargs']['float_features']"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: module 'torch.compiler' has no attribute 'config'
```

Now
```
>>> import torch
>>> torch.compiler.config.dynamic_sources = "L['kwargs']['float_features']"
```

messages.kimi:
docs: Fix incorrect documentation for `from_buffer` size constraint

The documentation for `torch.from_buffer` incorrectly stated that the buffer size must be "less than" the calculated size based on offset, count, and dtype. This contradicts the actual requirement that the buffer must contain enough data to read the specified number of elements. Changed "less than" to "more than" to accurately describe the constraint that the buffer size must exceed the offset plus count times dtype size.
messages.claude:
docs: fix incorrect buffer size condition in Tensor.frombuffer doc

The docstring for Tensor.frombuffer stated the buffer's total byte length
must be "less than" offset + count * dtype.itemsize when count is positive.
This is logically backwards — the requirement is that the buffer be large
enough to cover the requested slice, i.e. the total bytes must be *more
than* (greater than or equal to) that value. The previous wording led users
to believe valid buffers were being rejected and vice versa, causing
confusion when constructing tensors from raw memory. Correct "less than" to
"more than" so the documented precondition matches the actual validation
logic and user expectations.
messages.minimax:
docs: fix incorrect inequality in merge_dicts buffer documentation

The documentation for merge_dicts incorrectly stated "less than" when describing the buffer size constraint. The condition should check if buffer size is "more than" offset plus count times dtype size. This typo could have misled users about valid buffer parameter constraints.

messages.claude:
docs: document complex dtype sampling behavior in torch.randn and torch.randn_like

Adds documentation for how `torch.randn` samples complex dtypes, specifying that the output follows a complex normal distribution CN(0, 1) — equivalent to sampling the real and imaginary parts independently from N(0, 1/2). Updates the `torch.randn_like` description to reference `torch.randn` for the complex dtype sampling process rather than duplicating the explanation.

Why: The previous docs only described the real-valued sampling behavior, leaving the semantics of complex dtypes unspecified. Users had no way to know that complex samples are split evenly between real and imaginary components (variance 1/2 each) to preserve the unit-variance property of the overall complex tensor.
messages.kimi:
docs: Document complex dtype sampling behavior for torch.randn and torch.randn_like

Add comprehensive documentation explaining how complex dtypes are sampled from a complex normal distribution in torch.randn. The documentation now clarifies that complex values are i.i.d. sampled with zero mean and unit variance, equivalent to sampling real and imaginary parts independently from N(0, 1/2). Also update torch.randn_like to reference torch.randn for complex dtype sampling details.

This addresses the lack of clarity around complex number generation in the PyTorch documentation, helping users understand the statistical properties of randomly generated complex tensors.
messages.minimax:
docs: document complex dtype sampling behavior in torch.randn and randn_like

Adds mathematical notation explaining that for complex dtypes, torch.randn samples from a complex normal distribution CN(0,1), equivalent to sampling real and imaginary parts independently from N(0, 1/2). Updates randn_like to reference torch.randn for complex sampling details.

messages.kimi:
docs: Deprecate torch.set_default_tensor_type() and update documentation references

Add deprecation warning to torch.set_default_tensor_type() as of PyTorch 2.1, directing users to use torch.set_default_dtype() and torch.set_default_device() instead. Update all documentation references across the codebase to point to the new recommended functions. This change is part of the migration away from the legacy tensor type-based API toward the more explicit dtype and device-based API, providing clearer separation of concerns and better type safety.
messages.claude:
[Docs] Deprecate `torch.set_default_tensor_type` and update references to `torch.set_default_dtype`/`torch.set_default_device`

Adds a deprecation warning to `torch.set_default_tensor_type` as of PyTorch 2.1, directing users to `torch.set_default_dtype()` and `torch.set_default_device()` as the preferred alternatives.

Replaces stale references to `torch.set_default_tensor_type` throughout the docs and source comments. References that describe default dtype inference now point to `torch.set_default_dtype`, and references that describe default device selection now point to `torch.set_default_device`. Affected areas include the tensor creation docstrings in `torch/_torch_docs.py`, the sharded tensor and DTensor creation routines under `torch/distributed/`, and the inline comment in `torch/csrc/lazy/core/shape_inference.cpp`. The example demonstrating that `set_default_tensor_type` mutates the default dtype is also removed from the `set_default_dtype` docs, since the deprecated API should no longer be advertised as a supported way to influence default dtype.

Motivation: `torch.set_default_tensor_type` conflates dtype and device configuration into a single call, which is error-prone and hides intent. The dedicated `torch.set_default_dtype` and `torch.set_default_device` APIs make the two concerns explicit, and the documentation should steer users toward them rather than to the legacy combined API. Updating the cross-references ensures that users following the docs land on the recommended APIs, and the deprecation notice makes the upcoming removal discoverable.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/100099

Summary:
The LLVM warning `-Wmissing-field-initializers` has found one or more structs in this diff's files which were missing field initializers.

This can be unintended such as:
```
my_struct s1 = {0}; // Initializes *only* the first field to zero; others to default values
my_struct s2 = {}; // Initializes *all* fields to default values (often zero)
```
or it may be because only some of the members of a struct are initialized, perhaps because the items were added to the struct but not every instance of it was updated.

To fix the problem, I've either used `{}` to initialize all fields to default or added appropriate default initializations to the missing fields.

messages.kimi:
Based on the diff and reference examples, I can see this is a fix in the PyTorch distributed c10d TCPStore component. The change adds a call to `addMiscellaneousSocket(rawSocket)` when a new socket is accepted.

Looking at the pattern from the reference examples and the nature of this change:

fix: Add missing addMiscellaneousSocket call in TCPStoreMasterDaemon

The TCPStoreMasterDaemon::run() method was not calling addMiscellaneousSocket() when accepting new client connections. This omission could lead to improper socket tracking and resource management issues, as the socket would be added to the internal sockets_ vector and pollfd list but not registered with the miscellaneous socket tracking mechanism. Adding this call ensures consistent socket lifecycle management across all tracking structures.
messages.claude:
feat(c10d/TCPStore): track master daemon sockets via addMiscellaneousSocket

What:
Register each socket accepted by TCPStoreMasterDaemon::run() with
addMiscellaneousSocket(rawSocket) right after it is added to the poll
set, so the daemon's bookkeeping for miscellaneous sockets stays in
sync with the sockets_ vector.

Why:
Previously, sockets accepted by the master daemon were tracked in
sockets_ and the pollfd array but were not registered through
addMiscellaneousSocket. This left the daemon's socket-tracking state
inconsistent: any logic that relies on addMiscellaneousSocket (e.g.
clean shutdown / fd cleanup for non-worker sockets) would miss these
accepted connections, which could result in leaked file descriptors or
stale entries lingering after the daemon stops. Calling
addMiscellaneousSocket at the point of acceptance keeps the two
tracking paths consistent and ensures accepted sockets are torn down
correctly on shutdown.
messages.minimax:
c10d/TCPStore: track newly accepted sockets for proper cleanup

When a new socket connection is accepted in TCPStoreMasterDaemon::run(), the raw socket fd is now registered with addMiscellaneousSocket() alongside being added to the sockets_ vector and pollfd list. This ensures the socket is tracked in the miscellaneous tracking mechanism for proper lifecycle management and cleanup.

The code example in get_state_dict's docstring was not properly formatted for doctest execution. messages.claude:
docs: convert get_state_dict docstring example to xdoctest-skipped runnable form

Summary:
Converts the `get_state_dict` example in `torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py` from plain prose into `>>>` doctest format with `# xdoctest: +SKIP`, and adds an explicit `:rtype:` annotation to the Returns section.

Why:
The example previously used non-runnable code blocks (no `>>>` prefixes), so it was not picked up by xdoctest and was inconsistent with the rest of the codebase's doctest conventions. Rewriting it as a skipped doctest keeps the snippet syntax-highlighted and copy-pasteable while marking it as non-executable, since the snippet depends on a distributed initialization (rank/process group) that cannot run in a plain doctest environment. Adding the `:rtype:` field also improves the generated API reference and aligns with the typing improvements being made across the distributed checkpoint module.

Following the pattern of recent doc/typing follow-ups (e.g., #149942, #153386) that tidy up `state_dict` documentation for clarity and consistency.

ci: Update install_triton_wheel.sh to use different index URLs for release and nightly branches

The script now detects the current git branch and uses the appropriate PyTorch package index:
- For release branches: installs from test.pytorch.org (stable builds)
- For other branches: installs from nightly.pytorch.org with commit hash (development builds)

This ensures release branches get stable triton packages while development branches continue to use nightly builds with specific commit pins.
messages.claude:
[BE] install_triton_wheel.sh use test index for release branches

The script previously always installed pytorch-triton from the nightly index with a git-commit-suffixed version. On release branches the nightly wheel is not the right artifact and the commit-suffix is not present, so the pinned version lookup fails. Detect the current branch with `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` and route release branches to the `test` index (plain pinned version), while non-release branches keep the existing nightly behavior.

part 2 - fix strided sharding for uneven padding

this builds on the previous PR and corrects the full_tensor
reconstruction to account for padding in the case of strided
sharding with uneven tensor shape and padding.

Example:  (copied from _StridedShard._to_replicate_tensor docstring)
-------
mesh = (DP=2, TP=2)
original = torch.arange(5)

tp sharded tensor
-----------------
`tp = distribute_tensor(x, world_mesh['tp'], [Shard(0)])`

local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1,2]    rank1: [3,4]
rank1: [0,1,2]    rank3: [3,4]

fsdp+tp sharded tensor
----------------------
`dp_tp = ...` (the process of creating a strided-shard tensor is skipped over as it is hacky and complicated #TODO put an example somewhre and ref to it)
dp_tp has placement (_StridedShard(0, split_factor=2), Shard(0))
local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1]  rank1: [3]
rank1: [2]    rank3: [4]

Now, say someone wants to reconstruct dp_tp's full tensor. This will invoke 'redistribute' to replicate.
redistribute will first replicate the "Shard(0)" placement on the rightmost mesh dim, then replicate the
StridedShard placement second, which is implemented by this function.
So our starting point (`local_tensor` arg) is the result of replicating the Shard(0) placement across the
TP dim, which looks like this.

Note the discrepancy with the 'tp sharded tensor' line above!  We'll fix it by locally shuffling data.

local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1,3]  rank1: [0,1,3]
rank1: [2,4]    rank3: [2,4]

Step 1: replicate over the DP dimension.  Afterwards, each rank can locally sort the values.
  note: we need padding to do this allgather, and we'll need to keep track of the padding amount for later
	local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1,3,2,4]    rank1: [0,1,3,2,4]
rank1: [0,1,3,2,4]    rank3: [0,1,3,2,4]

Step 2: chunk and shuffle values around to account for the wrong order of operations above
and get the original tensor content back

01324#       <- our allgather includes padding, if padding was applied in step 1
01324        <- Remove the padding
013, 24      <- chunk once, 'undoing' the DP allgather
01, 3, 2, 4  <- chunk each chunk, 'undoing' the initial (wrong) TP allgather performed by Shard(0)->Replicate()
012, 34      <- interleave with stride=TP mesh dim size
01234        <- concatenate

messages.kimi:
feat: Enable FULL_STATE_DICT support with DeviceMesh for 2D FSDP + TP

Remove the RuntimeError and warning that prevented using FULL_STATE_DICT with device_mesh in 2D FSDP + TP configurations. The previous restriction was overly conservative - FULL_STATE_DICT can work correctly with DeviceMesh when there is a parent mesh, as the state dict handling properly manages the tensor sharding. This change allows users to use FULL_STATE_DICT with device_mesh without unnecessary warnings or errors, improving flexibility for distributed training setups that combine FSDP with Tensor Parallelism.
messages.claude:
fix: remove FULL_STATE_DICT warnings/errors for FSDP with device_mesh

Remove the warning in `_state_dict_utils.py` and `_optim_utils.py` that
fires when FULL_STATE_DICT is used together with device_mesh, and drop
the corresponding RuntimeError that blocked 2D FSDP+TP. Update the test
in `test_fsdp_dtensor_state_dict.py` to no longer assert on these
warnings.

Why: Previously, FSDP emitted a warning (or raised for 2D FSDP+TP)
whenever a user combined FULL_STATE_DICT with a device_mesh, nudging
them toward SHARDED_STATE_DICT. This restriction is being lifted so
that FULL_STATE_DICT works as expected in device_mesh / 2D FSDP+TP
setups. The old warning/error path is no longer reached, so keeping
the assertions would cause the test to fail; removing the dead warning
code keeps behavior consistent with the new supported configuration.

[DTensor][FSDP] Remove warnings/errors for FULL_STATE_DICT with device_mesh

Remove warnings when using FULL_STATE_DICT state_dict_type with device_mesh in both _optim_utils.py and _state_dict_utils.py. Also remove the RuntimeError for 2D FSDP + TP case (parent device_mesh) in _full_pre_state_dict_hook. These checks were blocking valid configurations that are now supported.

Prevent cudaStreamSync when indexing GPU tensors with boolean CPU mask (#156384)

`index_put` with a boolean mask (`target[mask] = src`) causes a `cudaStreamSynchronize`. When both `mask` and `target` tensors are on GPU this is expected.

However, the sync can be prevented if the `mask` is a CPU tensor.
Internally a new index tensor is created with `mask.nonzero()` so we can use a non-blocking copy to transfer it to the GPU since it cannot be accidentally mutated by the user between its creation and the device copy. @ngimel Let me know if I'm missing something.

I think this is useful since users can't prevent a sync simply by making sure all tensors are on the same device as with other ops. Instead one would need to do something like this which is much less readable
```python
indices = mask.nonzero().squeeze(1).to("cuda", non_blocking=True)
target[indices] = src
```
Fixes #12461

Cast to unsigned char to avoid UB (#152360)

The standard requires that the argument to functions like `isdigit`, `isalpha`, and similar must be either `EOF` or an `unsigned char`; otherwise, the behavior is undefined (UB).
To avoid out-of-bounds reads, modern implementations of some libraries (such as glibc) deliberately pad their internal tables to guarantee valid memory access even for negative values. However, this is implementation-specific, and other libraries may not do this.

Properly casting the argument to `unsigned char` is good practice to avoid potential issues on some platforms.

messages.claude:
fix: Enable mkldnn bf16/fp16 device check on MSVC x64 builds

The mkldnn bf16/fp16 device check functions (`mkldnn_bf16_device_check`
and `mkldnn_fp16_device_check` in aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/Utils.h)
were guarded by `#if defined(__x86_64__)`, which is the GCC/Clang
predefined macro for x86-64 targets. MSVC does not define `__x86_64__`;
instead it defines `_M_X64` for x64 builds. As a result, on Windows
builds compiled with MSVC the ideep-based support check was skipped
and the functions fell through to the `#else` branch returning `false`,
disabling bf16/fp16 support even on capable x64 hardware.

Extend the condition to `defined(__x86_64__) || (defined(_M_X64) &&
!defined(_M_ARM64EC))` so the ideep check is reached on MSVC x64
builds as well. The `!defined(_M_ARM64EC)` exclusion is necessary
because ARM64EC targets define `_M_X64` in addition to `_M_ARM64EC`,
but they are not genuine x86-64 and must not take the ideep/avx_ne_convert
code path.

This restores correct bf16/fp16 capability detection on Windows x64
builds using MSVC.

messages.kimi:
feat: Cache and reuse submesh slice results in DeviceMesh

Add parent-to-child mapping in _MeshEnv to cache submesh slice results and avoid creating duplicate process groups when the same mesh dimension is accessed multiple times. This improves performance by reusing existing child meshes instead of recreating them, and adds a test to verify the caching behavior works correctly for both cached and new slices.
messages.claude:
perf: cache and reuse child mesh slicing result to avoid duplicate process group creation

When slicing a DeviceMesh by mesh_dim_name (e.g. mesh["dp"]), the
implementation always called create_child_mesh, which creates a new
process group (pg) for the sub-mesh even when the same slice had
already been created before. Repeated slicing of the same dim in
long-running training workflows (common in DTensor/FSDP2/TP setups)
therefore leaked process groups and inflated _world.group_count, since
each redundant slice instantiated a fresh pg for the same set of ranks.

This adds a parent_to_child_mapping cache (Dict[DeviceMesh, Dict[str,
DeviceMesh]]) to _MeshEnv. create_child_mesh now short-circuits and
returns the existing sub-mesh when a slice for the given mesh_dim_name
already exists, and otherwise populates the cache after creating it.
child_to_parent_mapping is preserved for back-compat. This keeps
pg count stable across repeated slicing of the same dim, while still
allowing new pgs to be created when a previously-unsliced dim (e.g.
"tp") is requested for the first time.

Test:
`pytest test/distributed/test_device_mesh.py::TestDeviceMesh::test_cache_and_reuse_submesh_slice_result`
messages.minimax:
feat: cache submesh slices in DeviceMesh to avoid recreating child meshes

When slicing a DeviceMesh (e.g., `mesh["dp"]`), the child mesh and its associated
process group were being recreated on every access. This change adds a

Test added: `test_cache_and_reuse_submesh_slice_result` verifies that a second

a different dimension slice still creates new process groups as expected.

fix: [MPS] Fix clamp to propagate NaN values

Replaces `clampWithTensor` with a composition of `minimumWithNaNPropagationWithPrimaryTensor` and `maximumWithNaNPropagationWithPrimaryTensor` in the MPS clamp implementation. The previous `clampWithTensor` op does not propagate NaN through, which caused `torch.clamp` on MPS to diverge from CPU semantics when the input tensor contained NaN values (NaN should be preserved through clamp per the documented contract).

Handles all three code paths (min+max, max-only, min-only) consistently by chaining the min/max ops with NaN propagation so the result matches the CPU reference behavior across each case.

Adds `test_clamp_nan` to verify MPS and CPU produce equal results for inputs containing NaN across clamp with min+max, min-only, and max-only variants.

[MPS] Refactor fill_scalar_mps_impl to remove legacy macOS workarounds

Replace constantWithScalar with mpsGraphScalarPlaceHolder to eliminate
workarounds for bool/UInt8 types on macOS 12.3/12.4/Ventura. The old
implementation had special handling because constantWithScalar didn't
work properly for these types on older macOS versions. Using the
placeholder approach with proper scalar data feeding is cleaner and
removes technical debt from supporting outdated OS versions.

Also add nn.functional.rms_norm to supported MPS ops list.
messages.claude:
[MPS] Fix fill_scalar for bool/uint8 by using scalar placeholder instead of constantWithScalar

Replaces the `constantWithScalar` based implementation in `fill_scalar_mps_impl` with a scalar placeholder fed at run time, and removes the bool/uint8 casting workarounds that were needed because `constantWithScalar` did not work for these types on MacOS-12.[34] (see issues #82427 and #83692).

What:
- Add an `inputTensor_` placeholder to the CachedGraph and build the output via `identityWithTensor:` on the placeholder instead of `constantWithScalar:`.
- Feed the scalar value through `mpsScalar`/`getMPSGraphTensorFromScalar` at execution time, passing `feeds` to `runMPSGraph` instead of nil.
- Drop the Bool/UInt8 detection and subsequent `castTensor:` workarounds, since the placeholder path handles all scalar types uniformly.
- Register `nn.functional.rms_norm` in the MPS ops test modifier list.

Why:
The previous implementation relied on `constantWithScalar:shape:dataType:`, which is broken for Bool and UInt8 types on MacOS-12.3/12.4 and Ventura preview, forcing fragile cast workarounds (filed as #82427 and #83692). Baking the scalar into the graph also forced a graph cache miss for every distinct scalar value, since the cache key includes `value.toDouble()`. Using a scalar placeholder decouples the graph topology from the scalar value, so the cast workarounds are no longer needed and the cached graph can be reused across different scalar inputs, fixing correctness for bool/uint8 and improving cache reuse.
messages.minimax:
[MPS] Remove bool/UInt8 workarounds in fill_scalar_mps

The constantWithScalar workarounds for bool and uint8 types (filing as int8/uint32 then casting) were needed for MacOS-12.[34] and Ventura preview due to issues #82427 and #83692. These are no longer needed on current MacOS versions.

The fix replaces constantWithScalar with mpsGraphScalarPlaceHolder and passes the scalar as a feed to the graph, eliminating the type-specific casts and simplifying the code.

messages.kimi:
fix: Remove redundant checkpoint prefix handling in _get_fqns

The change consolidates checkpoint prefix removal to a single location at the start of `_get_fqns()` instead of handling it in multiple places. This fixes a bug where the prefix was being inconsistently processed - it was removed for simple names but not properly handled in the FSDP flat parameter path. By removing the prefix upfront, we ensure consistent FQN generation regardless of the code path taken, eliminating potential mismatches when checkpointing with FSDP-wrapped modules.
messages.minimax:
[BE][FSDP] Fix checkpoint prefix not removed in _get_fqns for compound names

The checkpoint prefix removal was only applied when "." was not in the name, causing compound FQNs to retain the _CHECKPOINT_PREFIX incorrectly. Moved the prefix stripping before the dot check to ensure consistent handling for all name forms.
messages.claude:
fix: remove checkpoint prefix from FQNs before FSDP wrapped module traversal

Move the _CHECKPOINT_PREFIX removal to the start of _get_fqns so it applies uniformly to all code paths. Previously the prefix was only stripped in the early-return branch for single-segment names, leaving it in place when the name contained "." and was traversed through FSDP's _fsdp_wrapped_module. This caused FQNs returned via the FSDP flat param path to still carry the checkpoint prefix, breaking state dict loading for prefixed checkpoints. Also drop the now-misleading comment claiming FSDP handles prefix removal itself.

messages.kimi:
fix(dcp): skip non-persistent buffers in state dict iteration

Non-persistent buffers (registered with persistent=False) were being
incorrectly included when iterating through module buffers in
get_model_state_dict(). This caused state dict mismatches when
loading models with non-persistent buffers, as these buffers should
not be part of the checkpoint.

The fix adds a check to skip buffers that are in the module's
_non_persistent_buffers_set when yielding FQN-object pairs.
messages.claude:
[DCP] Skip non-persistent buffers in state_dict traversal

Non-persistent buffers (registered with persistent=False) should be excluded from the distributed checkpoint state_dict, matching the behavior of Module.state_dict() which omits them by default. Previously, recurse() in state_dict.py iterated over all named_buffers and named_parameters without checking the _non_persistent_buffers_set, causing non-persistent buffers to leak into the DCP state_dict. This led to mismatches when round-tripping through get_model_state_dict/set_model_state_dict on DDP-wrapped models, since the restored keys would include buffers the user explicitly requested not to be saved.

The fix adds a guard to skip any buffer name present in module._non_persistent_buffers_set during traversal. A regression test (test_non_persistent_buffers) is added that registers a non-persistent buffer on a model, wraps it with DDP, and verifies the DCP state_dict matches Module.state_dict() after a round-trip.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/154000
messages.minimax:
[checkpoint] fix state_dict to skip non-persistent buffers

Non-persistent buffers (registered with `persistent=False`) are not saved in checkpoints and should be excluded from state_dict operations. This fix adds a check to skip buffers in `_non_persistent_buffers_set` when collecting state dict, preventing mismatches between model and checkpoint state during save/restore operations.

exemplars.message:
[Inductor][FlexAttention] fix `vars_and_sizes` divisor error (#151634)

Triton codegen currently [sorts vars by divisor](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L233-L237). When there are two vars with the same divisor, the order is undecided.

```python
nodes.sort(
   key=lambda x: V.graph.sizevars.size_hint(
       x.divisor, fallback=config.unbacked_symint_fallback
   )
)
```

The test case leads to the following nodes:
```
(Pdb) nodes[0]
IterationRangesEntry(x1, ((s37 + 127)//128), 2, (xindex//ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[1]
IterationRangesEntry(x0, 1, ((s37 + 127)//128), ModularIndexing(xindex, 1, ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[2]
IterationRangesEntry(x2, 2*(((s37 + 127)//128)), ((s12 + 127)//128), (xindex//(2*(((s37 + 127)//128)))), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].length, 2)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].length, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].length, 1)
True

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].divisor, 2)
True
```

Since x1 and x0 both have divisor 1, the relative order is random across runs.
In some runs, we have order [x1, x0, x2] with divisors as [1,1,2] and lengths as [2,1,1]. After x1, we have [divisor = divisor * node.length](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L246) = 1 * 2 = 2. Then, when processing x0, we have node.divisor=1, divisor=2, and [FloorDiv(node.divisor, divisor)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L251) = 0, which indicates an iteration length of 0 and leads errors later.

The fix is to sort by both divisor and length_is_one. So for two nodes with the same divisor, we process the node with length=1 first.

[Inductor][CPP] Fix Codegen Issue when Parallel Reduction under the vectorization (#151887)

**Summary**
Fixes [#151290](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/151290) and [#151523](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/151523), which are regressions introduced by [#144020](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/144020). That PR enabled parallelization at the inner loop level.

However, a currently unsupported case arises when parallel reduction occurs under the vectorization loop level, specifically in patterns like:
```
for vec_loop_level:
    do_parallel_reduction
```
In such cases, a temporary buffer `tmp_acc_array` is allocated for tail scalar kernels, and another temporary buffer `tmp_acc_array` is also defined for parallel reduction. This results in a conflict due to overlapping temporary buffers. This PR disables the problematic case to avoid the conflict until proper support is implemented.

messages.kimi:
refactor: Simplify MutationOutput dependency tracking by using direct input instead of WeakDep

The MutationOutput class currently tracks the node doing the mutating via a custom
get_read_writes() method that adds a WeakDep. This is unnecessarily complex and
can be simplified by passing node_doing_mutating directly as an input to the parent
class.

The change:
1. Passes node_doing_mutating as an input to super().__init__() instead of just
   mutated_node
2. Removes the custom get_read_writes() override since the dependency is now
   captured naturally through the inputs list

This makes the dependency tracking more explicit and reduces special-case handling
in the IR layer. The test updates (fudge factor for memory metrics and op counting
in MKL-DNN tests) accommodate the slightly changed behavior in generated code.
messages.minimax:
[Inductor] Fix MutationOutput dependency tracking for correct memory access counting

The `MutationOutput` class was not properly tracking `node_doing_mutating` as a dependency in its reads. Previously it only added a WeakDep via `get_read_writes()`, which did not properly integrate into the memory access counting. This caused the flex attention `num_bytes_accessed` test to fail with incorrect counts.

This fix:
1. Includes `node_doing_mutating` as a direct input in the `MutationOutput` constructor instead of a weak dependency
2. Updates the flex attention test to use a less strict assertion with a fudge factor to account for extra materialization that occurs alongside the mutation
3. Adds `num_include_ops` parameter to verify operator call counts in pattern matcher tests, with new test coverage for both CPP and Python wrapper paths
messages.claude:
[Inductor] Track mutation source as data dependency for memory planning

Summary
Modify `Mutation` IR node to include `node_doing_mutating` as an explicit
input rather than registering it as a `WeakDep` in `get_read_writes`.
This makes the mutation source a real data dependency, which lets the
scheduler correctly order passes and reason about memory access.

Why
Previously the dependency between a mutation and the node performing the
mutation was expressed via `WeakDep`, which is not treated as a hard
dependency by memory planning / scheduling. As a result, inductor
incorrectly materialized the attention output and emitted an extraneous
logsumexp write in the flex attention path (see the fudge factor and
TODO added in `test_flex_attention.py`).

Concretely, in `test_memory_pool` we now allow up to two extra accesses
(one for the unnecessary materialization tied to mutation, one for the
extraneous logsumexp write) instead of asserting an exact byte count
that no longer holds. The exact-count assertion was broken because the
mutation path caused two additional reads/writes that the previous
`WeakDep` modeling did not capture. We use `assertLess` rather than an
exact `assertEqual` since the fudge is a temporary upper bound until
the underlying materialization issue is fixed.

The same change also enables the cpp-wrapper path in
`test_mkldnn_pattern_matcher.py` to verify the expected onednn op
counts (`qlinear_pointwise` / `qlinear_pointwise.binary`) via a new
`num_include_ops` parameter, ensuring both python and cpp wrappers emit
exactly two of each op after the dependency fix.

Test Plan
- `python test/inductor/test_flex_attention.py -k test_memory_pool`
- `python test/inductor/test_mkldnn_pattern_matcher.py`

messages.kimi:
fix: Use dist.get_rank(group) instead of fsdp_state.rank for correct broadcast rank check

The code was incorrectly checking `fsdp_state.rank` to determine if the current process should be the source of broadcast operations. In distributed training with FSDP, `fsdp_state.rank` may not reflect the rank within the specific process group used for the broadcast. This change ensures the correct rank is obtained from `dist.get_rank(group)` for the specific process group being used, fixing potential issues where the wrong process attempts to broadcast or the broadcast source is incorrectly determined.
messages.minimax:
fix: use dist.get_rank(group) instead of fsdp_state.rank for group-local rank checks

The original code incorrectly used `fsdp_state.rank` to determine the source rank in broadcast operations. However, `fsdp_state.rank` reflects the global rank, not the rank within the specified `group`. When broadcasting with a non-default process group, rank 0 in that group may not correspond to rank 0 in `fsdp_state`. This bug could cause incorrect rank 0 checks when using custom process groups in FSDP state broadcasting operations.
messages.claude:
fix: use dist.get_rank(group) instead of fsdp_state.rank in FSDP broadcast helpers

Use the process group's rank rather than the FSDP state's rank when
determining which process is the broadcast source in
_broadcast_processed_state and _broadcast_state. fsdp_state.rank reflects
the global rank, which is incorrect when these helpers operate within a
sub-group (e.g., the non-default group created for hybrid sharding or
CPU offload). Using the global rank caused non-zero global-rank ranks
within a sub-group to be misidentified as rank 0, leading to incorrect
broadcast source selection and corrupted optimizer/tensor state across
the sub-group.

Replacing it with dist.get_rank(group) ensures the source rank is
resolved relative to the actual broadcast group, so the broadcast
semantics remain correct regardless of how FSDP state is partitioned
across process groups.

pr_title: Remove cuda check in the CUDAGraph destructor

exemplars.message:
Reland fast gather and index implementation (#151917)

This PR reapplies #151490 and #151753 together, and adds some missing checks when applying the fast path.
Previously missed checks:
1) indexing path has the stride in the indexed dimension in bytes, gather path has the stride in the indexed dimension in elements. When checking if fast path is applicable, I didn't take this difference into account, and still multiplied the indexing stride by element size. Fixed and test added
2) We want to take fast path only when we are copying contiguous equally spaced slices of inputs + all the necessary alignment requirements. The effective tensor size should be 2d (after all possible flattening is applied), the index stride in the last dimension should be 0, and, since in the kernel we are not applying non-indexing-related offsets to src tensor, the src tensor stride in the second dimension should be 0. This automatically happens for gather with dim=0, so I didn't put in an explicit condition for this. Sometimes all conditions except first dim "effective" stride equal to 0 are satisfied for scatter on non-zero dim, when index size in the indexing dimension is 1 and thus it is collapsed (dimensions of size 1 are always collapsed), e.g.
```
        # test gather along 1st dim that can accidentally trigger fast path
        # because due to index dimension in the gather dim being 1
        # an unexpected squashing in tensorIterator happens
        src = make_tensor((16, 2, 16), device=device, dtype=dtype)
        ind = torch.randint(2, (16, 1), device=device).view(16, 1, 1).expand(16, 1, 16)
        res = torch.gather(src, dim=1, index=ind)
        if res.device.type == "cuda":
            ref_cpu = torch.gather(src.cpu(), dim=1, index=ind.cpu())
            self.assertEqual(res.cpu(), ref_cpu, atol=0, rtol=0)
```
Note that if index size here was (16, 2, 16) instead of (16, 1, 16) then the middle dimension could not be collapsed and we wouldn't end up incorrectly taking fast path.
We could update the kernel to take this stride into account when computing offsets into src tensor, or we could specifically disallow non-zero stride on the first dimension. I took the second path for now.

Provide access to the cudaGraph_t underlying a CUDAGraph. (#155164)

There are a few considerations here:

1. A user might want to modify the cudaGraph_t either during the stream capture or after the stream capture (but before instantiation). This draft implements modification after stream capture only, though support could be added for modification during stream capture by applying
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/140979/files#diff-d7302d133bb5e0890fc94de9aeea4d9d442555a3b40772c9db10edb5cf36a35cR391-R404

2. Previously, the cudaGraph_t would be destroyed before the end of capture_end() unless the user had previously called enable_debug_mode(). There is no way to implement this correctly without removing this restriction, or forcing the user to always call enable_debug_mode(). However, enable_debug_mode() is a confusing API (despite being an instance method, it would modify a static global variable; thus, putting one CUDAGraph object into debug mode puts all of them into debug mode, which is not acceptable in my opinion). Therefore, I made enable_debug_mode() into a no-op. This means that the CPU memory usage will increase after this change. I think this is likely to be fine.

3. No python bindings yet. These should be easy to add. It is probably worthwhile to take some time to make sure that the returned cudaGraph_t can be converted into the cuda-python cudaGraph_t in a reasonable, hopefully type-safe, manner (but without making cuda-python a dependency of pytorch), since I imagine most users will use the pip cuda-python package to make modifications.

4. There are two foot guns:

   a. The cudaGraph_t returned by raw_cuda_graph() is not owned by the user, so it will be destroyed once the owning CUDAGraph is destroyed (or calls reset()).

   b. The following seuquence won't work as intended:

```
g = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
with torch.cuda.graph(g):
    foo()
g.replay()
raw_graph = g.raw_cuda_graph()
modify(raw_graph)
g.replay()
```

This won't work because the user must call instantiate() again after modifying cudaGraph_t. You could add a "safety" mechanism by traversing the cudaGraph_t to create a hash and seeing if the hash changes between calls to replay(), but this is likely way too expensive.

I think these two foot guns are probably okay given that this a bit of an experts' API.

fix: allow unregistering CUDA graph during capture

Removes the assertion that prevented unregistering a CUDA graph from
the RNG state while a stream capture is in progress. The previous
guard called at::cuda::assertNotCapturing(...) in
CUDAGeneratorState::unregister_graph, which would abort if a user
attempted to unregister a graph while capture was active.

be torn down (e.g., on exception or during cleanup) from within a

the registered graph entry. The remaining TORCH_CHECK on
registered_graphs_ still validates that the graph was previously
registered, so removing the capture guard does not weaken the
correctness invariants of registered_graphs_; it only lifts the
overly broad restriction on when unregister can be called.

messages.claude:
[NCCL] Expose `ncclRemoteError` in result enum mapping (#155379)

NCCL 2.27 introduced a new `ncclRemoteError` result type to signal failures
originating from a remote rank. PyTorch's wrapper enums (`ncclResult` in
`nccl.h` and the conversion helpers in `nccl.cpp`) only knew about
`ncclNumResults` and `ncclInProgress`, so a remote error returned by NCCL
would hit the `default` branch and throw "Unconvertible NCCL type" instead
of being surfaced to the caller.

Add `RemoteError` to the wrapper enum and map it to/from
`ncclRemoteError` in both `to_nccl_result` and `from_nccl_result`. The
`NumResults` entry is renumbered to 8 (it is a sentinel value marking the
end of the enum range) and moved after `InProgress` so the numeric order
matches the upstream NCCL `ncclResult_t` definition, preventing
accidental mis-indexing of future result codes.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/155379
Approved by: https://github.com/Skylion007
messages.kimi:
fix: Add ncclRemoteError to NCCL result enum and fix conversion mappings

The NCCL library defines ncclRemoteError as a valid error code (6) that
indicates a remote process failed or aborted. Previously, PyTorch's
ncclResult enum incorrectly mapped this value to NumResults, which is
meant to be a sentinel counting the number of results, not an actual
error code.

This change:
- Adds RemoteError = 6 to the ncclResult enum
- Renumber NumResults from 6 to 8 (after InProgress = 7)
- Updates to_nccl_result() and from_nccl_result() to properly convert
  ncclRemoteError instead of incorrectly mapping ncclNumResults

This ensures proper error handling when NCCL operations fail due to
remote process issues, allowing users to receive meaningful error
messages instead of "Unconvertible NCCL type" exceptions.

[aten] Enable vectorized 8byte copy for fp16/bf16 for index select kernel (#152380) ## Summary Enable aligned vector loading for 2 bytes data types for index select. Specifically: - **4 element fp16/bf16 packing**: added 8-byte vector load/store to move 4 half values at once. - **warp-wide predicate (__all_sync)**: decide fast vs fallback path per warp, eliminating lane level divergence - **alignment guard**: fast or vectorized path only executes when src and dst are 8 byte aligned, preventing mis aligned address faults. - **Safe for loop fallback**: for misaligned, strid > 1, or tail elements we recompute offsets per element to avoid memory corruption. - **Bound checks**: fast or vectorized path is skipped when less than 4 elements are remaining, guaranteeing bounded access. - **Stride remapping**: Redirect calls to inner contiguous dim which has stride = 1 so copies occur along memory coalesced axes. - **AMD support**: Ensured portability and correctness across CUDA and HIP platforms. ## Perf testing We note a 2.5x improvement in memory bandwidth after this change when the tensor dim is a multiple of 4 for 2 byte data types (fp16/bf16). Currently, `torch._chunk_cat` only supports contiguous inputs (due to `.view()` usage in `_pad_chunk()` supporting only contiguous tensor). This doesn't work for internal models where there can be non-contiguous input tensors:

Reland fast gather and index implementation (#151917)

This PR reapplies #151490 and #151753 together, and adds some missing checks when applying the fast path.
Previously missed checks:
1) indexing path has the stride in the indexed dimension in bytes, gather path has the stride in the indexed dimension in elements. When checking if fast path is applicable, I didn't take this difference into account, and still multiplied the indexing stride by element size. Fixed and test added
2) We want to take fast path only when we are copying contiguous equally spaced slices of inputs + all the necessary alignment requirements. The effective tensor size should be 2d (after all possible flattening is applied), the index stride in the last dimension should be 0, and, since in the kernel we are not applying non-indexing-related offsets to src tensor, the src tensor stride in the second dimension should be 0. This automatically happens for gather with dim=0, so I didn't put in an explicit condition for this. Sometimes all conditions except first dim "effective" stride equal to 0 are satisfied for scatter on non-zero dim, when index size in the indexing dimension is 1 and thus it is collapsed (dimensions of size 1 are always collapsed), e.g.
```
        # test gather along 1st dim that can accidentally trigger fast path
        # because due to index dimension in the gather dim being 1
        # an unexpected squashing in tensorIterator happens
        src = make_tensor((16, 2, 16), device=device, dtype=dtype)
        ind = torch.randint(2, (16, 1), device=device).view(16, 1, 1).expand(16, 1, 16)
        res = torch.gather(src, dim=1, index=ind)
        if res.device.type == "cuda":
            ref_cpu = torch.gather(src.cpu(), dim=1, index=ind.cpu())
            self.assertEqual(res.cpu(), ref_cpu, atol=0, rtol=0)
```
Note that if index size here was (16, 2, 16) instead of (16, 1, 16) then the middle dimension could not be collapsed and we wouldn't end up incorrectly taking fast path.
We could update the kernel to take this stride into account when computing offsets into src tensor, or we could specifically disallow non-zero stride on the first dimension. I took the second path for now.

fix: resolve integer overflow in CUDA index operations for large tensors (>=2GB)

When tensor sizes reach 2147483648 (2GB), the signed `ptrdiff_t` type causes overflow in several places within `index_add_cuda_impl`, `index_reduce_func_cuda_impl`, and `index_select_out_cuda_impl`. Additionally, on ROCm the `std::min` specialization does not behave correctly for values >= 2147483648, leading to incorrect block dimension calculations and potential memory access issues.

Changes:
- Convert `getSliceSize` return type and local slice size variables from `ptrdiff_t` (signed) to `uint64_t`/`size_t` (unsigned) to prevent overflow
- Replace `std::min` with a ternary conditional for `largeIndexBlock` calculation to avoid ROCm std::min edge case
- Add regression test with 40GB large tensor (131072 indices × 16384 embedding dim = 2147483648 output elements)

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/130806
messages.kimi:
fix: Fix integer overflow in CUDA indexing operations for large tensors (#130806)

Summary

Fix integer overflow issues in CUDA indexing operations by changing signed integer types (`ptrdiff_t`, `int64_t`, `int`) to unsigned types (`size_t`, `uint64_t`). This resolves failures when operating on tensors with more than 2^31 elements.

Details

- Changed `getSliceSize` return type from `ptrdiff_t` to `size_t` since slice sizes are always non-negative
- Updated local variables in `index_add_cuda_impl`, `index_reduce_func_cuda_impl`, and `index_select_out_cuda_impl` from `ptrdiff_t`/`int64_t`/`int` to `uint64_t` for consistency and to prevent overflow
- Fixed `dim3` grid/block calculations to use `uint64_t` instead of `ptrdiff_t` when computing thread configurations
- Added explicit bounds check for `largeIndexBlock` to handle cases where `outTotalSize >= 2147483648` on ROCm, where `std::min` -> `::min` did not work as expected with signed types
- Added test case `test_large_tensors` to verify embedding operations work correctly with tensors containing 2,147,483,648 elements (40GB GPU memory requirement)

The root cause was that `ptrdiff_t` is a signed type, and when `outTotalSize` reaches 2,147,483,648 (2^31), it would overflow the signed integer range, causing incorrect behavior in grid/block size calculations and potentially leading to CUDA kernel launch failures or incorrect results.

messages.claude:
fix: Resolve integer overflow in CUDA index_select and index_add kernels for large tensors

Summary

Replaces signed `ptrdiff_t` (and mixed `int64_t`) with unsigned `uint64_t`/`size_t` for slice size, total size, dim size, numel, and grid/block dimension computations in `index_add_cuda_impl`, `index_reduce_func_cuda_impl`, and `index_select_out_cuda_impl` (and the helper `getSliceSize`). Adds a regression test in `test_embedding.py` exercising a 2B-element embedding output.

Why

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/130806 — `F.embedding` (and other index ops) crashed or produced incorrect results when the output tensor had `>= 2^31` elements.

Two root causes:

1. Signed integer overflow: `ptrdiff_t` is a signed 32-bit-wide type on the relevant targets. An `outTotalSize` of 2147483648 overflows `ptrdiff_t` at `INT_MAX + 1`, producing a negative value. This negative value then flowed into `std::min(sliceSize, (ptrdiff_t)128)` for grid/block sizing, yielding invalid launch dimensions. Switching these variables to `uint64_t` (and `size_t` for `getSliceSize`'s return/locals) makes them unambiguously hold the full unsigned range of `numel()`/`size()`.

2. ROCm `std::min` behavior: On ROCm, `std::min` did not behave as expected when the operand was `>= 2147483648` (the 2^31 boundary), compounding the overflow above. For `largeIndexBlock` we replace the `std::min(outTotalSize, (uint64_t)128)` call with an explicit ternary `(outTotalSize < 128) ? outTotalSize : 128` to sidestep the platform-specific `min` quirk entirely. The comment is preserved in-tree to flag the ROCm-specific workaround for future readers.

The cast sites for `ceil_div(...)` and the `mpc * 8` upper bound are updated to `uint64_t` to keep the types consistent across the `std::min` operands and avoid new sign-comparison warnings.

Test

Adds `test_large_tensors` in `test/nn/test_embedding.py`, decorated with `@largeTensorTest("40GB", device="cuda")`, which builds a `[131072]` long index tensor and a `[16032, 16384]` weight, runs `F.embedding`, and asserts the output is 2-d with `numel() == 2147483648` — the exact boundary that triggered the original overflow.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add missing arithmetic and bitwise operators for VSX vectorized types

Add C10_ALWAYS_INLINE operator overloads (+, -, *, /, &, |, ^) for all VSX vectorized types including float, double, complex float, complex double, int16, int32, int64, qint8, quint8, and qint32. Also add vec0()/vec1() accessor methods to Vectorized<ComplexFlt> for consistency with other vectorized types.

These operators are required to enable proper vectorized operations on PowerPC VSX architecture, ensuring that arithmetic and bitwise operations can be performed efficiently using the underlying VSX intrinsics (vec_add, vec_sub, vec_mul, vec_div, vec_and, vec_or, vec_xor).
messages.claude:
feat: add vectorized binary operators for VSX backend

Implement the missing arithmetic (+, -, *, /) and bitwise (&, |, ^) operator overloads for the PowerPC VSX Vectorized specializations across all supported dtypes: float, double, complex float, complex double, int16, int32, int64, qint8, qint32, quint8. Also expose vec0()/vec1() accessors on the ComplexFlt class so these operators can construct results from the underlying vector registers.

Previously these operator templates were only declared but not defined for the VSX path, leaving VSX builds dependent on the generic (non-vectorized) fallbacks and preventing the vectorized code path from being exercised. Defining them with the corresponding vec_add/vec_sub/vec_mul/vec_div/vec_and/vec_or/vec_xor intrinsics ensures VSX-capable POWER systems emit native vector instructions and produce correct, performant results consistent with the existing scalar operators.
messages.minimax:
Add missing arithmetic and bitwise operator implementations for VSX vectorized types

Summary:
Adds template specializations for `operator+`, `operator-`, `operator*`, `operator/`, `operator&`, `operator|`, and `operator^` to Vectorized<T> types in the VSX (PowerPC Vector Scalar Extension) backend.

Why:
The VSX vectorized types were missing implementations for fundamental arithmetic and bitwise operators that exist in other backends (e.g., AVX). Without these operators, code using vectorized arithmetic on PowerPC would either fail to compile or fall back to slow scalar paths. This change enables vectorized computation for float, double, int16, int32, int64, qint32, qint8, quint8, ComplexFlt, and ComplexDbl types on VSX-capable hardware.

Changes to HFStorageWriter to support saving shards of tensors (#154742) (#155566)

Summary:

As we move towards supporting saving partial tensors natively with HFStorageWriter, there are some simple changes that need to be made to make this happen.
- The current approach for distributed writes is that every rank has full tensors, but we split up the writing of these full tensors across all available ranks. We're removing this logic that was in the HFSavePlanner and instead assuming that every rank has a shard and saving every rank's local state
    -  as a result we can probably remove the HFSavePlanner, but keeping it as a placeholder for now

- the current naming of files doesn't support shards as its in the format "model-00001-of-00004.safetensors", but if every rank is writing the same file names they will overwrite eachother, so this adds a shard-00001 prefix, so that the rank files don't overwrite eachother
- don't save the metadata file models.safetensors.index.json if sharding is enabled. This file expects a 1 to 1 ratio between tensor and filename, but this doesn't make sense in the sharded saving approach, so we can just get rid of this file
- make the "fqn_to_file_index" map optional. This is to describe which files to save which tensors in, but if users don't want to provide this, we can just save all the tensors to one file. If they run into issues, they can choose how to split up their tensors to be more friendly with 5GB HF remote storage file size soft limit.

fix: Add weights_only parameter to torch.load calls in distributed checkpointing

The changes add explicit `weights_only` parameter to all `torch.load()` calls in the distributed checkpointing module. This addresses PyTorch 2.6+ deprecation warnings where `weights_only` defaults to True, which breaks loading of certain checkpoint formats that contain non-tensor objects. from False to True, which would break loading checkpoints containing
non-tensor objects (e.g., stateful objects, custom types).

- filesystem.py: weights_only=True where only raw tensors are loaded

messages.kimi:
Based on the code changes, I can see this is a bug fix for handling infinity values in the CPU Flash Attention kernel. The change adds a check for `tmp_max == -std::numeric_limits<accum_t>::infinity()` to avoid NaN results from `exp2f(-inf - (-inf))`. A test case was also added to verify the fix for issue #127055.

fix: Handle -inf values in CPU Flash Attention softmax computation

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/127055.

When attention mask contains -inf values (e.g., causal masking), the softmax computation in cpu_flash_attention could produce NaN due to exp(-inf - (-inf)). This occurred when tmp_max was -infinity and we tried to compute exp(qk_max_data[row] - tmp_max).

Fix:
Add a conditional check before the exponential computation. When tmp_max is -infinity, fill the output with zeros directly instead of computing the exponential and reduction. This avoids the undefined behavior of exp(-inf - (-inf)) = NaN.

Test:
Added test_scaled_dot_product_fused_attention_with_inf to verify that Flash Attention produces the same results as the math backend when using attention masks with -inf values.
messages.claude: pytest test/test_transformers.py -k test_scaled_dot_product_fused_attention_with_inf
messages.minimax:
[CPU] Fix flash attention NaN when attention mask is all -inf (#127055)

What: Add check for `-inf` max value in CPU flash attention kernel before computing exponentials.

Why: When the attention mask contains all `-inf` values (e.g., `torch.full((600, 600), float("-inf"))`), the softmax computation produces `nan = exp(-inf - (-inf))` due to undefined behavior when subtracting negative infinity from itself. The fix handles this edge case by filling with zeros instead of attempting the exponential computation.

How: Added a conditional check at `FlashAttentionKernel.cpp:354` that detects when `tmp_max == -infinity` and uses `fill_stub` to zero out the row before the softmax calculation, matching the expected mathematical result where attention weights on an all-`-inf` mask should be zero.

[CUDAGraph Trees] support memory allocation on side stream (#152472)

I tried `beginAllocateToPool` instead of `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentStreamToPool` and the error in #151199 does not happen any more.

However, this approach is unsafe for multithreading. When multiple run_eager happens concurrently, we expect memory allocation to different mem_pool. Since beginAllocateToPool does not check stream, these memory allocation may happen on the same mem_pool.

So, I use `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool` to direct all memory allocation on the same thread to a given mem_pool. In particular, `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool` records the launching thread id, and during runtime checks if the current thread id matches the launching thread id.

Fixes #151199

Based on the code changes and the issue reference (#133520), I can see this is fixing a bug where batch normalization on MPS was producing incorrect results when operating on tensor slices. The fix removes an incorrect optimization that was skipping the gather operation for contiguous tensors.

fix: [MPS] Fix batch norm incorrect results on tensor slices (#133520)

Removes the incorrect `executeGatherOp` optimization that was skipping the gather operation when the input tensor was contiguous. This optimization was causing incorrect results when batch normalization operated on non-contiguous slices of tensors, as the MPS graph expected properly strided data.

The fix ensures that the gather operation is always performed, allowing the Placeholder to correctly handle the input tensor's memory layout regardless of contiguity.

Fixes #133520
messages.claude:
fix: [MPS] Fix batch norm for sliced inputs

Fixes #133520

Previously, batch norm on MPS would produce incorrect results when given a
non-contiguous sliced input (e.g. `x[5:]`). The code unconditionally rewrote
the memory format to Contiguous and skipped the gather op whenever the input
was contiguous in the requested memory format, which caused the placeholder
to misinterpret the strided slice and feed the wrong data into the kernel.

This change removes the early `executeGatherOp` override so that sliced inputs
are always gathered correctly, and adds a regression test comparing MPS output
against CPU for a sliced `BatchNorm2d` input.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/133521
Approved by: https://github.com/malfet
messages.minimax:
[MPS] Fix batch_norm incorrect result with sliced tensors (#133520)

The issue was in the batch norm MPS implementation where the `executeGatherOp` flag was incorrectly set to `false` for contiguous inputs. This caused incorrect results when computing batch norm on sliced tensors (e.g., `x[5:]`) because the gather operation needed for non-contiguous tensor views was being skipped. Removed the conditional logic that forced `executeGatherOp=false` for contiguous inputs, ensuring sliced tensors are properly handled. Added regression test to verify batch norm produces correct results on MPS compared to CPU for sliced inputs.

We could technically use `alloca` to stack allocate instead of heap allocate, though in my tests it didn't seem to affect runtime performance on benchmarks particularly impressively, and alloca has portability issues, so I'd rather just stick with something simpler for now.

part 2 - fix strided sharding for uneven padding

this builds on the previous PR and corrects the full_tensor
reconstruction to account for padding in the case of strided
sharding with uneven tensor shape and padding.

Example:  (copied from _StridedShard._to_replicate_tensor docstring)
-------
mesh = (DP=2, TP=2)
original = torch.arange(5)

tp sharded tensor
-----------------
`tp = distribute_tensor(x, world_mesh['tp'], [Shard(0)])`

local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1,2]    rank1: [3,4]
rank1: [0,1,2]    rank3: [3,4]

fsdp+tp sharded tensor
----------------------
`dp_tp = ...` (the process of creating a strided-shard tensor is skipped over as it is hacky and complicated #TODO put an example somewhre and ref to it)
dp_tp has placement (_StridedShard(0, split_factor=2), Shard(0))
local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1]  rank1: [3]
rank1: [2]    rank3: [4]

Now, say someone wants to reconstruct dp_tp's full tensor. This will invoke 'redistribute' to replicate.
redistribute will first replicate the "Shard(0)" placement on the rightmost mesh dim, then replicate the
StridedShard placement second, which is implemented by this function.
So our starting point (`local_tensor` arg) is the result of replicating the Shard(0) placement across the
TP dim, which looks like this.

Note the discrepancy with the 'tp sharded tensor' line above!  We'll fix it by locally shuffling data.

local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1,3]  rank1: [0,1,3]
rank1: [2,4]    rank3: [2,4]

Step 1: replicate over the DP dimension.  Afterwards, each rank can locally sort the values.
  note: we need padding to do this allgather, and we'll need to keep track of the padding amount for later
	local_tensors:
rank0: [0,1,3,2,4]    rank1: [0,1,3,2,4]
rank1: [0,1,3,2,4]    rank3: [0,1,3,2,4]

Step 2: chunk and shuffle values around to account for the wrong order of operations above
and get the original tensor content back

01324#       <- our allgather includes padding, if padding was applied in step 1
01324        <- Remove the padding
013, 24      <- chunk once, 'undoing' the DP allgather
01, 3, 2, 4  <- chunk each chunk, 'undoing' the initial (wrong) TP allgather performed by Shard(0)->Replicate()
012, 34      <- interleave with stride=TP mesh dim size
01234        <- concatenate

fix: resolve stateless optimizer handling and correct zero_grad/step ordering in checkpoint state_dict tests

The zero_grad() calls were incorrectly placed after step() instead of before, which caused issues for stateless optimizers like SGD. Additionally, _init_optim_state was incorrectly raising an error when gradients exist for stateless optimizers - these optimizers don't have state to initialize, so existing gradients should not block state_dict operations. Also adds SGD to the optimizer test matrix to catch similar issues earlier.
messages.kimi:
1. Main changes in `torch/distributed/checkpoint/state_dict.py`:
   - Modifies `_init_optim_state` function to handle stateless optimizers like SGD
   - Previously, it would raise a RuntimeError if gradients existed but optimizer states weren't initialized
   - Now it returns early if gradients exist, allowing stateless optimizers (like SGD without momentum) to work
   - The change allows SGD to work with `state_dict` even though it doesn't have persistent state

2. Test changes in `test/distributed/checkpoint/test_state_dict.py`:
   - Adds SGD to the test parametrization for FSDP, DDP tests
   - Changes learning rate from 1e-3 to 1e-4
   - Reorders optimizer step/zero_grad calls for consistency

3. Test utility changes in `torch/testing/_internal/distributed/common_state_dict.py`:
   - Improves error message when tensor comparison fails

The core issue being fixed is that SGD (a stateless optimizer when used without momentum) would fail when calling `state_dict` because the code assumed all optimizers need state initialization. The fix allows SGD to work properly.

Based on the allowed commit types, this is a fix - it's fixing a bug where stateless optimizers like SGD couldn't be used with distributed checkpoint state_dict.

fix: Allow stateless optimizers (e.g., SGD) to work with distributed checkpoint state_dict

The _init_optim_state function previously raised a RuntimeError when gradients existed but optimizer states weren't initialized. This prevented stateless optimizers like SGD (without momentum) from working with distributed checkpointing, as they don't maintain persistent state.

Change the logic to return early when gradients exist, allowing stateless optimizers to bypass state initialization. Also add SGD to the test coverage and improve error messages for debugging tensor mismatches.
messages.claude:
fix: support stateless optimizers like SGD in distributed checkpoint state_dict

What:
- Remove the RuntimeError in `_init_optim_state` when gradients are
  already present; instead return early since the optimizer state is
  effectively initialized.
- Add SGD to the FSDP/DDP test matrices and lower the learning rate
  from 1e-3 to 1e-4 across state_dict tests.
- Fix the training loop in `_test_save_load` to zero gradients for all
  optimizers before backward and step them after, handling both single
  optimizer and list-of-optimizers cases.
- Improve `_verify_msd` error messages to include the FQN and tensor
  values on mismatch.

Why:
Stateless optimizers such as SGD do not maintain explicit optimizer
state, so the previous guard that raised a RuntimeError whenever
`param.grad is not None` incorrectly blocked legitimate checkpoint
flows where gradients exist but there is nothing to initialize. This
made it impossible to use `state_dict` with SGD after a backward pass.
The early return preserves the existing zero-grad initialization path
for stateful optimizers (e.g. Adam/AdamW) while leaving SGD untouched,
since with zero gradients and the configured lr the SGD step is a
no-op. The learning rate is reduced to 1e-4 because SGD diverges with
the previous 1e-3 setting, causing numerical mismatches between the
original and distributed optimizers in `_test_save_load`; the lower lr
keeps Adam/AdamW stable as well. The training-loop reordering ensures
gradients are properly cleared each iteration for all optimizer
variants (including optim-in-backpack), preventing stale-gradient
accumulation that would also break the state_dict comparison.

messages.minimax:
[ROCm] Use modern CMake imported targets for HIP libraries

Update HIP library linking to use CMake imported targets (hip::amdhip64, MIOpen, hiprtc::hiprtc, roc::hipblaslt) instead of raw library variables. This replaces PYTORCH_HIP_LIBRARIES and PYTORCH_MIOPEN_LIBRARIES with proper CMake targets, and adds hiprtc as a required HIP dependency discovered via find_package.
messages.claude:
[ROCm][build] Modernize HIP dependency linking with CMake imported targets (#158357)

Replace manual `find_library` lookups and raw variable-based linking with
CMake imported targets (e.g., `hip::amdhip64`, `hiprtc::hiprtc`, `roc::hipblaslt`,
`MIOpen`) across `c10/hip/CMakeLists.txt`, `cmake/Dependencies.cmake`, and
`cmake/public/LoadHIP.cmake`.

Why:
- Imported targets propagate usage requirements (include paths, compile
  definitions, transitive deps) more reliably than flat library variables,
  reducing link-order and missing-symbol issues that have historically bitten
  the ROCm build (cf. the rocsolver undefined-symbol fix in #156591 and the
  hiprtc/cmake-4 workaround in #150324).
- `hiprtc` was not being found via `find_package` before; this change adds the
  `hiprtc_DIR` hint and `find_package_and_print_version(hiprtc REQUIRED)` call,
  making the dependency explicit and consistent with how other ROCm packages
  are discovered.
- Linking `c10_hip` against `c10` directly is replaced by the `C10_LIB` target
  so it stays in sync with the canonical c10 target definition.
- `roc::hipblaslt` is appended individually (rather than via a `list(APPEND ...)`
  on a variable that may be empty) to avoid silently dropping the dependency
  when the upstream exported target is unavailable.

feat: Update AOTriton to 0.7b with Navi31 support and CUDA graph-safe RNG

Implement CUDA graph-safe RNG state handling for dropout in flash attention, using philox state tensors instead of scalar values during stream capture. Update GPU compatibility checks and error messages to include Navi31. Adjust test tolerances for ROCm and disable GQA tests on ROCm until full support is available.
messages.minimax:
Add Navi31 (gfx1100) GPU support to AOTriton SDPA integration

This commit adds support for Navi31 GPUs (gfx1100) to the AOTriton-based
scaled dot product attention implementation. Key changes:

- Updated aotriton version from 0.6b to 0.7b and switched from bz2 to gz
  compression format for the release artifacts
- Added new adapter functions `mk_aoscalartensor` and `mk_philoxtensor` to
  properly handle tensor views for scalar values and philox RNG state
- Implemented CUDA graph-safe RNG state handling: when in capture stream,
  pass philox state pointers directly to attn_fwd/attn_bwd instead of
  scalar tensors, allowing proper RNG state capture and replay
- Added Navi31 (gfx1100) to the list of supported GPUs with experimental
  flag `TORCH_ROCM_AOTRITON_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL=1` to enable it
- Disabled grouped query attention on ROCm (backend doesn't support it yet)
- Updated test fudge factors for ROCm to account for different numerical
  precision characteristics, and adjusted test parameters (disable GQA on
  ROCm, adjust causal options for fp32)
messages.claude:
feat: Update AOTriton to v0.7b and add Navi31 (gfx1100) GPU support for SDPA

What:
- Bump AOTriton pin from 0.6b to 0.7b (new commit/SHA256, tarball format switched from .tar.bz2 to .tar.gz)
- Extend AOTriton-accelerated SDPA (flash + mem-efficient attention) to support Navi31 (gfx1100) GPUs, gated behind the TORCH_ROCM_AOTRITON_ENABLE_EXPERIMENTAL env flag
- Update error messages in attention.cu, attention_backward.cu, and flash_api.hip to advertise the newly supported arch (gfx90a/gfx942/gfx1100)
- Refactor philox RNG state handling: introduce mk_aoscalartensor/mk_philoxtensor adapters so the forward path can pass seed/offset as either an at::Tensor scalar (eager) or a raw philox pointer (CUDA Graph capture path), avoiding host-device syncs during graph capture
- Always allocate seed_t/offset_t on CUDA for ROCm to keep them usable from device-side kernels
- Disable GQA (grouped query attention) on ROCm by setting backend_supports_grouped_query_attention=false, since AOTriton does not yet support it
- Adjust test tolerances and skip/parametrize behavior in test_transformers.py and common_methods_invocations.py for ROCm (looser fudge factors, disable GQA parametrization, skip is_causal when seq_len_q != seq_len_k, skip fp32+causal combinations)

Why:
- AOTriton 0.7b is required to pick up Navi31 support and the new aten_fwd/aten_bwd API that accepts seed/offset/offset2/seed_output/offset_output as TensorView<0> rather than raw uint64 values. The new API is necessary for CUDA Graph compatibility: the previous implementation dereferenced seed_t.data_ptr<int64_t>() on the host, which forces a host-device sync and breaks graph capture. Passing philox state pointers directly during capture (use_philox_state) lets the kernel read RNG state at launch time without breaking out of capture.
- Navi31 support is marked experimental (env-gated with a TORCH_WARN_ONCE) because the AOTriton kernels work but have not yet met the numerical-stability bar required to enable by default. This matches the upstream AOTriton project's stabilization cadence for RDNA3.
- GQA is disabled on ROCm because AOTriton's flash/mem-efficient kernels do not yet handle non-equal num_heads between Q and KV. Enabling it would silently route to the math fallback, which would change numerical behavior and break gradient tolerances in unexpected ways; explicitly disabling forces a clear, consistent fallback path.
- Test tolerances on ROCm were loosened because AOTriton's RDNA3/MI300 kernels accumulate in fp16/bf16 with slightly different reduction orders than the CUDA flash-attention reference, producing larger gradient deltas at longer sequence lengths and in fp32. The per-seq_len/per-dtype fudge factors reflect measured empirical bounds rather than a blanket relaxation.
- Skipping is_causal when seq_len_q != seq_len_k on ROCm is required because AOTriton's causal implementation assumes square attention windows; passing is_causal=True with mismatched lengths produces incorrect masking.
