fix: Expand assertion node removal to cover async/scalar/metadata assert ops in ONNX exporter

The `remove_assertion_nodes` FX pass previously only stripped
`aten._assert_async.msg` and `sym_constrain_range_for_size.default`, but the
assertion family in ATen also includes `_assert_async.default`,
`_assert_scalar.default`, and `_assert_tensor_metadata.default`. Models that
emit these variants (e.g. one containing `torch.ops.aten._assert_async.msg`
without the `.msg` overload, or the scalar/metadata variants) would leave
stray assertion call_function nodes in the graph after the pass, breaking
ONNX export with unexpected op errors.

Add the missing targets to `aten_assertion_targets` so all assertion-shaped
nodes are removed consistently, and add a regression test that exports a model
containing `_assert_async.msg` to guard against regressions.
messages.kimi:
fix: Expand aten assertion nodes removal in ONNX exporter to handle zero-output operations

The ONNX exporter's `remove_assertion_nodes` pass was only handling a limited set of aten assertion operations. This caused export failures when models contained other assertion variants like `_assert_async.default`, `_assert_scalar.default`, and `_assert_tensor_metadata.default` which have zero outputs and should be stripped during export.

This change adds the missing assertion targets to the removal set and includes a test case to verify that models with these assertions can be exported successfully.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES support for AMD GPU device visibility

Add support for ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES environment variable alongside HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES for AMD GPU device selection. ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES is processed first by the ROCm runtime, reducing the available GPU pool that HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES can select from. When both are set, HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES takes precedence but must not specify more devices than ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES allows.

The change ensures proper handling of device visibility on AMD systems where both environment variables may be configured, with validation to catch misconfigurations where HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES lists more devices than ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES permits.
messages.minimax:
[AMD] Add ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES support to _parse_visible_devices

Summary: Add support for `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` environment variable (HIP's underlying runtime) in device enumeration. When set, it limits the number of available AMD GPUs. If both `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` and `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` are set, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` takes precedence but is validated against the ROCR limit.

Why: AMD ROCm stack uses ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES as a lower-level env var that restricts GPUs before HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES is applied. Without handling ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES explicitly, device count and selection could be inconsistent between the two env vars. This change ensures proper device enumeration on AMD GPUs and adds validation when both env vars are used together.

Test: Added test cases for ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES with various HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES combinations.
messages.claude:
feat: support ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES in HIP visible device parsing

What:
- Parse `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` alongside `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` in `torch/cuda/__init__.py::_parse_visible_devices`
- When only `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` is set, return the full range of visible device indices
- When both env vars are set, validate that `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` does not exceed the ROCR count, then prefer `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES`
- Add test cases in `test/test_cuda.py::test_hip_device_count` covering ROCR-only and ROCR+HIP configurations

Why:
ROCm exposes two independent visibility knobs: `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (handled by the ROCr runtime, processed first) and `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES` (applied on top of the ROCR-filtered set). PyTorch previously honored only `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES`, so users who relied on `ROCR_VISIBLE_DEVICES` to restrict the device pool got incorrect device counts and indices. When both env vars are set, the previous code silently ignored ROCR, which could produce out-of-range indices or mismatched device counts relative to what the ROCr runtime actually exposes. This change makes PyTorch's view of visible devices consistent with the ROCr runtime's behavior, and adds a sanity check to surface misconfiguration as an explicit `RuntimeError` rather than a silent incorrect mapping. Test coverage is extended to lock in the new semantics for both ROCR-only and ROCR+HIP scenarios.

exemplars.message:
[Inductor][FlexAttention] fix `vars_and_sizes` divisor error (#151634)

Triton codegen currently [sorts vars by divisor](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L233-L237). When there are two vars with the same divisor, the order is undecided.

```python
nodes.sort(
   key=lambda x: V.graph.sizevars.size_hint(
       x.divisor, fallback=config.unbacked_symint_fallback
   )
)
```

The test case leads to the following nodes:
```
(Pdb) nodes[0]
IterationRangesEntry(x1, ((s37 + 127)//128), 2, (xindex//ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[1]
IterationRangesEntry(x0, 1, ((s37 + 127)//128), ModularIndexing(xindex, 1, ps0), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) nodes[2]
IterationRangesEntry(x2, 2*(((s37 + 127)//128)), ((s12 + 127)//128), (xindex//(2*(((s37 + 127)//128)))), {x0: ((s37 + 127)//128), x1: 2, x2: ((s12 + 127)//128), x4: 2*(((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128)), x5: 0, x6: 2, x7: (((s12 + 127)//128))*(((s37 + 127)//128))})

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].length, 2)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].length, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].length, 1)
True

(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[0].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[1].divisor, 1)
True
(Pdb) V.graph.sizevars.statically_known_equals(nodes[2].divisor, 2)
True
```

Since x1 and x0 both have divisor 1, the relative order is random across runs.
In some runs, we have order [x1, x0, x2] with divisors as [1,1,2] and lengths as [2,1,1]. After x1, we have [divisor = divisor * node.length](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L246) = 1 * 2 = 2. Then, when processing x0, we have node.divisor=1, divisor=2, and [FloorDiv(node.divisor, divisor)](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/ae6f6b8efb6380a94621d61100ffb05dab05db27/torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py#L251) = 0, which indicates an iteration length of 0 and leads errors later.

The fix is to sort by both divisor and length_is_one. So for two nodes with the same divisor, we process the node with length=1 first.

messages.kimi:
fix: Correct batch index in FlexAttention score_mod and mask_mod for NestedTensor

The batch index `b` passed to `score_mod` and `mask_mod` callbacks was always 0 when using NestedTensor with FlexAttention. This happened because the original batch index was being used instead of the nested batch index derived from `q_seq_idx`.

The fix extracts `b_nested = q_seq_idx[q_idx]` and passes it to the original modifier functions instead of the flat batch index `b`. This ensures that batch-specific logic in user-defined score_mod and mask_mod functions works correctly with NestedTensor inputs.

Added regression tests to verify that batch-specific modifications now produce different outputs than identity modifications, preventing silent incorrect behavior.

Fixes #143788
messages.minimax:
fix: pass correct nested batch index to score_mod and mask_mod

In nested tensor flex_attention, the `nt_score_mod` and `nt_mask_mod` wrapper
functions were incorrectly passing the outer batch index `b` (which is always 0
for nested tensors since they appear as a single batch from the outer perspective)
to the user's score_mod/mask_mod functions. This caused batch-specific
score_mods and mask_mods to receive `b == 0` regardless of the actual nested
sequence's batch index.

The fix extracts the correct nested batch index via `b_nested = q_seq_idx[q_idx]`
and passes that to `orig_mod_func` instead of the outer `b`.

Fixes #143788
messages.claude:
fix: pass nested batch index to score_mod/mask_mod in flex_attention for NestedTensor

When flex_attention is used with a NestedTensor, the wrapper functions
`nt_score_mod` and `nt_mask_mod` translate the flat `q_idx`/`kv_idx` into
nested indices (`q_nested`, `kv_nested`) so that user-supplied modifiers
operate on per-sequence coordinates. However, the batch index `b` was
being passed through unchanged from the flat call, which means it always
reflected the outer (flattened) batch dimension rather than the actual
batch a given query token belongs to.

Concretely, for a NestedTensor the batch dimension is folded into the
sequence dimension, so `b` seen by the user's `score_mod`/`mask_mod` was
effectively always 0 (or otherwise unrelated to the real batch index of
the token). Any modifier that depends on `b` — e.g. adding a per-batch
bias or masking based on `b == 0` — would silently produce wrong results
because every token appeared to belong to the same batch.

Fix this by deriving `b_nested = q_seq_idx[q_idx]` (the batch index of
the query token's sequence) and passing `b_nested` to `orig_mod_func`
in both `nt_score_mod` and `nt_mask_mod`, mirroring how `q_nested` and
`kv_nested` are already remapped.

Also add regression tests in `test_nestedtensor.py` that exercise
batch-specific `score_mod` and a `mask_mod` conditioned on `b == 0`,
asserting that the output differs from the identity/always-b==0 case.
These guards directly catch the bug where the batch index passed to the
modifier is incorrect.

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/143788

messages.minimax:
[Inductor-CPU] Support dynamic shapes for BMM with epilogue fusion

Add dynamic shape support for batch matrix multiply (BMM) operations with
epilogue fusion in the CPP backend. This enables proper sizevar handling
when batch dimensions are dynamic, preventing variable renaming issues
in GEMM templates.

Changes:
- cpp_bmm_template.py: Pass free sizevars from BY to GEMM templates so
  variables are not renamed in the BMM definition. Changed Y to Y_2d
  in output bindings for GEMM stubs.
- cpp_gemm_template.py: Use has_free_symbols() instead of is_symbol to
  detect dynamic batch size, and use size_hints() for both view_size and
  view_stride to properly handle dynamic dimensions.
- test_cpu_select_algorithm.py: Add tests for BMM with pointwise ops
  and reshape, BMM epilogue with dynamic reshape, and BMM with dynamic
  batch stride.

Enables cpp epilogue fusion counter and select_algorithm_autotune for
dynamic shape BMM cases.
messages.claude:
[Inductor][CPP] Support dynamic shapes in BMM epilogue fusion

Summary

Extend the CPP BMM/GEMM template codegen to handle dynamic batch
dimension and dynamic strides, so that epilogue-fused BMM kernels no
longer assume fully static shapes. This unblocks autotuned
(select_algorithm) CPP epilogue fusion for models that mark the batch
dimension as dynamic via `torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic`.

The prior code only inferred a dynamic batch size B from the input
tensor product (`view_size[0]`) and asserted the remaining dims were
static, leaving strides untouched. When B *and* the M/N stride carried
free symbols, the generated kernel referenced sizevars that were not
passed into the BMM def_kernel, causing variable renaming/lookup
mismatches in the generated C++.

Why

- Fixes dynamic-shape BMM cases (e.g. `[B, 8, M, K] @ [B, 8, K, N]`
  with `mark_dynamic(u, 0)`) that previously failed or generated
  incorrect kernels during CPP epilogue fusion.
- Adds three regression tests covering dynamic batch + static inner
  dims, a real-world bmm-epilogue dynamic-reshape graph, and a bmm
  where both B and M dimensions are dynamic with a transposed weight
  stride.
- Mirrors the dynamic-shape support already present in the Triton
  codegen path, bringing CPP wrappers to parity for these cases.

Changes

- `cpp_bmm_template.py`: pass all sizevars referenced in `BY` (output
  size + stride) through `extra_sizevars` to `def_kernel`, and emit
  `Y_2d` as the kernel output (instead of `Y`) so the 2D flattening
  used by the single-threaded/threaded MM stubs stays consistent.
  Collects `BY_sizevars` from the free symbols of `BY.get_size()` and
  `BY.get_stride()`.
- `cpp_gemm_template.py`: in `maybe_to_dense`, generalize the
  dynamic-batch handling from `view_size[0].is_symbol` to
  `has_free_symbols(view_size)`, and resolve both the size and stride
  via `sizevars.size_hints` (rather than only patching
  `view_size[0]`). This handles the case where the stride also carries
  free symbols (e.g. transposed weights under a dynamic M dim).
- `test_cpu_select_algorithm.py`: add
  `test_bmm_with_pointwise_with_reshape_dynamic_shapes`,
  `test_bmm_epilogue_dynamic_reshape`, and `test_bmm_dynamic_bm_stride`
  to lock in the new behavior, asserting that
  `select_algorithm_autotune` and `cpp_epilogue_fusion_counter` fire
  exactly once.

fix: [Inductor][CPP] Fix BMM with dynamic shapes by passing sizevars to GEMM templates

The BMM template was not properly handling dynamic shapes because size variables present in the output tensor were being renamed in the generated kernel code. This caused failures when batch dimensions were marked as dynamic using `torch._dynamo.mark_dynamic()`.

The fix passes all sizevars from the output tensor (both from size and stride) to the GEMM templates via `extra_sizevars`, preventing variable renaming issues. Additionally, the GEMM template now uses `size_hints()` to properly resolve dynamic view sizes and strides instead of manual tensor size inference.

This enables BMM operations to work correctly with dynamic batch dimensions, as verified by the new test cases covering various dynamic shape scenarios including reshape operations and permuted tensors.

messages.kimi:
fix: Skip ops already in decomposition_table to avoid overwriting critical decompositions

The change adds a check to skip adding ops to the decomposition table if they're already present. This prevents `torch._decomp.decomposition_table` from overwriting decompositions in `torch.export.default_decompositions`, which are more critical to torch.onnx.export. The comment clarifies that while the former covers more ops, the latter takes precedence for ONNX export compatibility.
messages.claude:
fix: skip already-registered ops when building ONNX decomposition table

The create_onnx_friendly_decomposition_table function was unconditionally
overwriting decomposition_table[op_overload] with the ONNX-specific decomp
function, even when the op was already present in the table. This caused
existing decompositions (notably those from torch.export.default_decompositions
and the ONNX registry, which are more critical to torch.onnx.export) to be
clobbered by later entries.

By skipping op_overloads that already exist in the table, we preserve the
existing decompositions while still adding new ones. This keeps custom ops
specified in the registry from being incorrectly decomposed during ONNX export,
aligning the ONNX-friendly table behavior with the expectation that registered
decompositions take precedence.

This ensures decompositions from torch._decomp.decomposition_table (which covers more ops
than torch.export.default_decompositions) are preserved, preventing custom ops specified
in the custom_translation_table from being incorrectly decomposed during ONNX export.

messages.kimi:
fix: Support large matrix multiplication on MPS by tiling when output exceeds 2^32 elements (#141909)

The MPS backend previously threw an error when matrix multiplication output exceeded 2^32 elements due to 32-bit indexing limitations. This change implements a tiling strategy that splits both the batch dimension and the row dimension when necessary, allowing matmul to work with larger tensors. The fix adds row-wise tiling logic to handle cases where the largest supported batch size becomes zero, ensuring the computation is properly chunked to stay within MPS limits.
messages.claude:
fix: support tiled matmul on MPS when output exceeds 2^32 elements

Adds row-tiling to tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl so that when a single
matmul's element count exceeds the 2^32 Metal indexing limit, the
computation is split both across the batch dimension and the row
dimension of the input/result tensors. When largestSupportedBatchSize
collapses to zero (i.e. one matrix alone exceeds the limit), we now
fall back to per-matmul tiling with up to 512 rows per tile, and
allocate separate last-tile descriptors to handle the remainder.

Also relaxes the upfront TORCH_CHECK that rejected any matmul whose
output exceeded 2^32 elements: the path now only asserts that no
individual output dimension exceeds 2^32, since larger outputs are
handled by the tiled implementation. This previously hit a hard error
on MPS for cases like torch.randn(1,1,72250) @ torch.randn(1,72250,1)
on half precision, where the intermediate tile size crossed the
threshold.

Adds test_large_matmul covering that scenario (issue #141909).

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/141909
messages.minimax:
[MPS] Fix matmul for large matrices exceeding 32-bit indexing limit

When matrix dimensions are large enough that `floor(pow(2, 32) / elemInMatrix)` evaluates to zero, the batch tiling strategy alone is insufficient. This change adds row/column tiling to handle cases where the largest supported batch size is zero, enabling matmul operations with very large output dimensions to work correctly on MPS devices.

Fixes issue #141909

[regression] Fix pin_memory() when it is called before device lazy initialization. (#149033)

Add HostAllocator as the unified parent class (#151431)

# Motivation
This PR introduces a unified parent class `HostAllocator` with the following goals:
1. Enable backend-specific host allocator registration, including support for out-of-tree backends.
2. Provide a unified and extensible API surface for host memory management across all backends, especially accelerators.

The new interface includes:
- `at::getHostAllocator()->allocate`
- `at::getHostAllocator()->empty_cache`
- `at::getHostAllocator()->record_event`
- `at::getHostAllocator()->get_stats`
- `at::getHostAllocator()->reset_accumulated_stats`
- `at::getHostAllocator()->reset_peak_stats`

# Additional Context
We plan to deprecate legacy APIs such as `at::cuda::CachingHostAllocator_emptyCache` and recommend users migrate to the new backend-specific API, for example:
```cpp
at::getHostAllocator(at::kCUDA)->empty_cache();
```
This refactor will help standardize host memory management across devices and simplify backend integration in the future.
Another key improvement I am going to do is move the `is_pinned` functionality into the `HostAllocator` class, which enables centralized pinned memory verification through calls like `at::getHostAllocator(at::kCUDA)->is_pinned(ptr)`.
Benefits include:
 - Consistent host memory handling across all device backends
 - Decouple pinned memory functionality with `AcceleratorHooksInterface` in a more modular way
 - Clearer separation between device memory allocation and pinned host memory management

This architecture makes the system more maintainable and extensible for future device support.

messages.kimi:
Looking at the code changes and the reference examples, I can see this is a bug fix related to pinned memory initialization.

The diff shows:
1. In `Context.h`, `getPinnedMemoryAllocator()` now calls `lazyInitDevice()` before returning the allocator
2. In `EmptyTensor.cpp`, the explicit `lazyInitDevice()` call is removed from `GetCPUAllocatorMaybePinned()` since it's now handled in `getPinnedMemoryAllocator()`

This matches exactly with Example 1, which describes the same issue: when `pin_memory()` is called before device lazy initialization, `is_pinned` returns false because the device isn't initialized. The fix moves lazy initialization to `getPinnedMemoryAllocator()`.

fix: Fix pin_memory() when called before device lazy initialization

Move lazy device initialization to getPinnedMemoryAllocator() to ensure the device is properly initialized before pinning a tensor. Previously, when pin_memory() was called separately from tensor creation, lazy device init was not triggered causing is_pinned to always return false.
messages.claude:
fix: move lazy device init into getPinnedMemoryAllocator to ensure device is initialized before pinning

What:
- In `aten/src/ATen/Context.h`, `getPinnedMemoryAllocator` now resolves a
  fallback accelerator device type (via `at::getAccelerator()`) when none is
  passed in, and calls `lazyInitDevice` on it before returning the allocator.
- In `aten/src/ATen/EmptyTensor.cpp`, `GetCPUAllocatorMaybePinned` no longer
  performs the `lazyInitDevice` + `getAcceleratorHooksInterface().getPinnedMemoryAllocator()`
  dance itself; it delegates to `Context::getPinnedMemoryAllocator`, which now
  owns both the lazy-init and the allocator lookup.

Why:
PR #145752 added an `isPinnedPtr` check that requires the device to be
initialized before a tensor can be reported as pinned, and triggered lazy
device init when `at::empty` was called with `pin_memory=True`. But that only
covered the case where the tensor is created pinned up front. When a tensor is
created first and pinned later via a separate `pin_memory()` call, no lazy init
was triggered, so `is_pinned` would always return false (issue #149032).

By moving the lazy initialization into `getPinnedMemoryAllocator`, every code
path that needs a pinned-memory allocator — including the separate
`pin_memory()` path via `GetCPUAllocatorMaybePinned` — is guaranteed to
initialize the device first. Consolidating the lazy-init + allocator lookup
into a single function also removes a duplicated code path and ensures the
device is initialized before the `isPinnedPtr` check runs, regardless of how
the pinned tensor was created.

Fixes #149032
messages.minimax:
fix: ensure device lazy initialization in getPinnedMemoryAllocator

When pin_memory() was called before device lazy initialization, it would always return false because the device was not initialized. This moves the lazyInitDevice call into getPinnedMemoryAllocator() so the device is guaranteed to be initialized before retrieving the pinned memory allocator, regardless of which code path triggers it. This fixes the case where a tensor is first created and then pinned via a separate pin_memory() call.

Fixes #149032

messages.kimi:
build: Lower ARM architecture requirement for SVE256 from armv8.2-a to armv8-a

Change the -march flag from armv8.2-a+sve to armv8-a+sve for SVE256 CPU
capability compilation. This broadens compatibility to ARM processors that
support SVE but don't require the full armv8.2-a architecture level, allowing
PyTorch to build and run on a wider range of ARM-based systems while still
utilizing SVE vectorization when available.
messages.claude:
build: fix SVE256 CPU capability march flag for broader toolchain compatibility

Summary
- Updated cmake/Codegen.cmake to use `-march=armv8-a+sve` instead of
  `-march=armv8.2-a+sve` for the SVE256 CPU capability build flags,
  applying the change to both Clang and non-Clang code paths.

Why
`-march=armv8.2-a+sve` requires a toolchain (compiler/assembler) that
recognizes the `armv8.2-a` architecture level. Older or non-LLVM
toolchains — notably GCC releases and some NDK/Android toolchains — do
not accept `armv8.2-a` as a march value and fail the build with an
"unrecognized argument" error, even when SVE itself is supported.

`armv8-a+sve` is the lowest common denominator that still enables the
SVE extension (via the `+sve` feature) on every toolchain that supports
SVE, while remaining compatible with `armv8.2-a`-only environments. The
`-msve-vector-bits=256` flag and the `-DCPU_CAPABILITY_SVE` define are
unchanged, so the runtime SVE256 capability behavior is preserved.

This mirrors the kind of toolchain-compatibility fix seen in
pytorch@148362, where an overly narrow build condition broke builds on
Android/GraceHopper systems, and broadening it restored compatibility
without changing intended behavior.
messages.minimax:
build: relax ARM SVE architecture from armv8.2-a to armv8-a

Relax the ARM architecture requirement for SVE vector extension from armv8.2-a to armv8-a in Codegen.cmake. The armv8.2-a variant is too restrictive and causes build failures on systems where only the base armv8-a architecture is available. This change ensures SVE support can be enabled on a broader range of ARM hardware while maintaining vectorization capability.

messages.claude:
[MPS] fix attention enable_gqa crash on mps

Fixes #149132

The MPS SDPA math kernel did not support grouped-query attention (GQA), causing a crash when enable_gqa=True was passed with mismatched query/key head counts. The kernel's fallback path silently assumed query, key, and value shared the same number of heads, so the non-divisible case produced undefined behavior.

This change adds an explicit head-count divisibility check in the MPS dispatch: when GQA is enabled and query has more heads than key, the key/value tensors are expanded via repeat_interleave along the head dimension before being forwarded to _scaled_dot_product_attention_math_for_mps. A matching TORCH_CHECK is also added inside the math kernel to surface a clear error if head counts ever diverge.

Test coverage added via test_sdpa_enable_gqa covering float16/float32 and is_causal True/False on the mps device.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/149147
Approved by: https://github.com/malfet

fix: Prevent global scratch space injection for non-Triton kernel calls in TMA descriptor generation

The `generate_args_decl` method was unconditionally injecting a global scratch space argument for all kernel calls. However, TMA descriptor initialization calls `initNDTMADescriptor`, which is not a Triton kernel and should not receive this additional argument.

fix: don't inject global scratch arg into non-triton kernel calls

generate_args_decl unconditionally injected the cpp_global_scratch arg at
the front of the arg list. That arg is specific to triton kernels and
should not be appended to calls that are not triton kernels — notably
initNDTMADescriptor invoked from generate_tma_descriptor, which is not a
triton kernel and was receiving a spurious leading scratch argument.

Add an is_triton_kernel flag (defaulting to True for backwards
compatibility) to generate_args_decl and gate the scratch-arg injection
on it. Pass is_triton_kernel=False from generate_tma_descriptor so the
TMA descriptor init call gets the correct argument list. Also document
the method's behavior and the new flag.

messages.claude:
fix: refactor path lookup in _preload_cuda_deps to fix CUDA library resolution

What: Extract the CUDA dependency path lookup logic into a new helper
function `_get_cuda_dep_paths` that returns both `nvidia/<lib_folder>/lib/<lib_name>`
and `<lib_folder>/lib/<lib_name>` candidates in one pass, and simplify the
loop in `_preload_cuda_deps` to break as soon as a candidate is found.

Why: Previously the loop short-circuited on the first iteration where
`path/nvidia` existed, falling back to `path/lib_folder/lib` only when no
nvidia-prefixed match was found. This made the search order depend on
whether `path/nvidia` happened to exist, rather than on which candidate
actually contained the library — causing `_preload_cuda_deps` to miss
valid CUDA libraries and raise spurious "not found" errors. By gathering
both candidate paths unconditionally and selecting the first match, the
lookup correctly resolves the library regardless of the directory layout,
fixing the bug reported in #149806.

Fixes #149806

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/149808
Approved by: https://github.com/jansel

messages.kimi:
fix: [MPS] Fix tril op handling of NaN and Inf values

The tril operation on MPS was incorrectly propagating NaN and Inf values from the upper triangle into the output. The original implementation used subtraction with a complement tensor, which caused NaN/Inf values in masked positions to affect the result through arithmetic operations.

Replace the subtraction-based masking with an explicit select operation that uses a boolean mask to choose between the input tensor and a zero tensor. This ensures values outside the lower triangle are explicitly set to zero without arithmetic involvement.

Add comprehensive tests for NaN, positive infinity, and negative infinity cases to prevent regression.
messages.minimax:
fix: tril op on MPS not handling inf/nan correctly

Fixes incorrect behavior in `torch.tril` on MPS backend when input tensors contain `inf`, `-inf`, or `nan` values. The previous implementation used subtraction to compute the lower triangular mask, which produced incorrect results for special values. The fix uses a conditional select based on whether the complement tensor equals zero, ensuring correct propagation of inf/nan values. Also adds regression tests covering these edge cases.
messages.claude:
[MPS] Fix tril to correctly handle inf/nan inputs

Replaces the subtraction-based complement approach with a select-based
mask so that inf and nan values in the input are preserved instead of
being corrupted by the arithmetic with the complement tensor.

Previously the tril implementation computed the output as
`input - complement`, where complement is zero inside the kept lower
triangle and -1 elsewhere. When the input contained inf, this produced
inf - 0 = inf inside the triangle (correct) but inf - (-1) = inf outside
(it should be 0), and nan propagated through both regions since
nan - x = nan. As a result tril on MPS disagreed with the CPU result for
inf/-inf/nan inputs.

The fix builds a boolean mask from the complement tensor
(`complement == 0`) and uses MPSGraph's `selectWithPredicateTensor:` to
pass through the original input value where the mask is true and write
zero where it is false. This avoids any arithmetic on the input, so inf
is preserved inside the triangle and zeroed outside, and nan no longer
leaks into the lower-triangular output.

Adds test coverage in test_mps.py that runs tril with diagonal values
0, 1, and -2 on tensors filled with inf, -inf, and nan, asserting
parity with the CPU implementation. Also collapses the existing
diag-loop test cases into a single loop for brevity.

messages.claude:
fix: quote include dirs path on Windows for correct MSVC argument parsing

On Windows, the previous `/I {inc_dir}` argument did not quote the
path, so any include directory containing spaces (e.g. a user-space
home dir or a conda env path like `C:\Program Files\...`) would be
incorrectly tokenized by MSVC, breaking the inductor C++ build. Wrap
the include directory in double quotes (`/I "{inc_dir}"`) so the
compiler receives the path as a single argument regardless of spaces.
messages.minimax:

messages.kimi:
fix: Use sysconfig to reliably locate Python libs on Windows

The previous approach of constructing the Python library path from
sys.executable could fail in certain Python installation configurations
(e.g., virtual environments, conda installations). Use sysconfig.get_path()
with the "nt" scheme to properly resolve the include directory and derive
the libs path from it, which is the standard and more robust method for
locating Python installation paths across different Windows setups.
messages.claude:
fix: derive Windows python lib path from sysconfig instead of sys.executable

On Windows, the previous approach located the `libs` directory by taking
the dirname of `sys.executable`. This is fragile because it assumes the
Python executable lives directly inside the root that also contains the
`libs` folder. In environments where the executable is placed elsewhere
(e.g. conda/poetry/venv layouts, embedded Python, or custom install
prefixes), `os.path.dirname(sys.executable)` does not point at the
prefix, so `libs` cannot be found and the inductor C++ build fails to
link against the Python library.

Use `sysconfig.get_path("include", scheme="nt")` (which resolves to
`<prefix>/include`) and take its parent to robustly recover the install
prefix, then append `libs`. This matches how sysconfig itself locates
the include dir and works across the Windows install layouts that
CPython supports, rather than relying on the executable's location.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add Default BlasBackend with automatic ROCm architecture detection

Add a new `Default` variant to `BlasBackend` enum that uses heuristics to automatically select the optimal BLAS backend based on GPU architecture. On ROCm, AMD Instinct targets (gfx90a, gfx942, gfx950) now default to hipBLASLt while other architectures use hipBLAS. This simplifies backend selection for users and ensures optimal performance on supported hardware without manual configuration.

The change also unifies environment variable handling for CUDA and ROCm, allowing both `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_CUBLASLT` and `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT` to work across platforms, and adds `hipblas` as an alias for `cublas` in the Python API.
messages.minimax:
feat: introduce Default BlasBackend with runtime heuristics

Introduce a new `BlasBackend::Default` enum value that defers backend selection to runtime heuristics, rather than hardcoding at compile time.

On CUDA systems, Default resolves to cuBLAS. On ROCm systems, Default resolves to hipBLASLt for Instinct architectures (gfx90a, gfx942, gfx950) and cuBLAS for all others.

Additionally, normalize environment variable handling by treating `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_CUBLASLT` and `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT` as aliases for the same logical preference, since hipblas maps to Cublas and hipblaslt maps to Cublaslt in the public API.
messages.claude:
feat: introduce BlasBackend::Default with heuristic-based selection for ROCm

Adds a new `Default` value to the `BlasBackend` enum so that the preferred BLAS library can be resolved lazily through heuristics rather than being pinned at construction time.

What:
- Adds `BlasBackend::Default` to the enum, its `BlasBackendToString` case, the Python binding, and the `.pyi` stub.
- Reworks `Context::blasPreferredBackend()` so that, when the preferred backend is still `Default`, it resolves to a concrete value once: `Cublaslt` on AMD Instinct targets (gfx90a/gfx942/gfx950) under ROCm, otherwise `Cublas`. The resolved value is cached back into `blas_preferred_backend` so call sites never have to interpret `Default` themselves.
- Adds a `hipblaslt_preferred` fast-path in the ROCm branch (mirroring the existing `hipblaslt_unsupported` check) and switches both loops from `getNumGPUs()` to `detail::getCUDAHooks().deviceCount()`, with the same substitution in `setROCmFABreferredBackend`.
- Exposes `"default"` (and `"hipblas"` as an alias of `"cublas"`) in `torch.backends.cuda.preferred_blas_library`, and documents that `"default"` defers to heuristics.
- Simplifies the env-var initialization in `Context.h`: `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT` is now accepted as an alias of `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_CUBLASLT`, `TORCH_LINALG_PREFER_HIPSOLVER` as an alias of `TORCH_LINALG_PREFER_CUSOLVER`, and an unset BLAS var no longer picks a backend explicitly — it leaves `blas_preferred_backend` at `Default` so the runtime heuristic can decide.
- Allows `setBlasPreferredBackend` to accept `Default` (warn-once only for the genuinely non-default choices).
- Adds `test_preferred_blas_library_settings` covering the default-resolution path, alias/env-var overrides, and error handling for bad inputs.

Why:
- Previously the BLAS backend was chosen eagerly from env vars at Context construction, which meant there was no way to express "pick the right library automatically based on the actual hardware present." On ROCm in particular, hipBLASLt is only beneficial on specific Instinct architectures (gfx90a/gfx942/gfx950); forcing a global default either left non-Instinct users on an unsupported backend or required every user to set `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT` manually.
- `Default` lets PyTorch defer the decision until the first `blasPreferredBackend()` call, where device properties are queryable, and resolve to `Cublaslt` on supported Instinct targets and `Cublas` everywhere else. Caching the result preserves the existing contract that the value is stable after first read.
- Treating `TORCH_BLAS_PREFER_HIPBLASLT`/`TORCH_LINALG_PREFER_HIPSOLVER` as aliases removes a long-standing ROCm papercut where users had to know to set the cuBLASLt-named variable on an AMD stack, while keeping the existing CUDA names working unchanged.
- Switching to `detail::getCUDAHooks().deviceCount()` keeps the device enumeration consistent with the surrounding `isGPUArch` calls (which already go through the hooks), which matters on builds where CUDA may not be directly linked.
- The new test guards both the resolution heuristic and the alias behavior so future changes to the default-selection logic are caught.

Enable aligned vector loading for 2 bytes datatypes in torch.cat. Specifically:

2. enable through a conditional template

The reason why 8-byte vector loading was chosen for fp16 and bf16:
16-byte load results in heavier register overheads (i.e. 4 register per load for fp32 -> 8 register per load for fp16). Therefore, to employ the benefits of vectorized loading, we reduced ALIGNED_VEC_LOAD_BYTES to 8 for fp16 and bf16

# pyre-strict
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

import click
import pandas as pd

import torch

# @manual=//triton:triton
import triton

# CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICEs=7 buck2 run @mode/opt //scripts/zhaozhu:cat_bench

@click.command()
@click.option("--data-type", type=str, default="bf16")
@click.option("--return-result", type=bool, default=False)
def main(
    data_type: str,
    return_result: bool,
) -> Optional[Tuple[List[triton.testing.Benchmark], List[pd.DataFrame]]]:
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    if data_type == "fp32":
        dtype = torch.float32
    elif data_type == "fp16":
        dtype = torch.float16
    elif data_type == "bf16":
        dtype = torch.bfloat16
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported data type: {data_type}.")

    D1 = int(torch.randint(low=10000, high=50000, size=(1,)).item())
    D2 = int(torch.randint(low=100, high=1000, size=(1,)).item())
    D3 = int(torch.randint(low=500, high=1000, size=(1,)).item())

    configs: List[triton.testing.Benchmark] = [
        triton.testing.Benchmark(
            x_names=["B"],
            x_vals=[100, 1000, 10000, 20000],
            line_arg="provider",
            line_vals=["pt_eager", "copy"],
            line_names=["pt_eager", "copy"],
            styles=[("blue", "-"), ("green", "-"), ("red", "-")],
            ylabel="ms",
            plot_name=f"torch-cat-D1-{D1}-D2-{D2}-D3-{D3}-dtype-{dtype}",
            args={
                "D1": D1,
                "D2": D2,
                "D3": D3,
                "dtype": dtype,
            },
        )
    ]

    @triton.testing.perf_report(configs)
    def bench_cat(
        B: int,
        D1: int,
        D2: int,
        D3: int,
        dtype: torch.dtype,
        provider: str,
    ) -> float:
        warmup = 10
        rep = 3

        tensors = []

        a = torch.empty(
            # (B, 30108),
            (B, D1),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)
        b = torch.empty(
            # (B, 624),
            (B, D2),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)
        c = torch.empty(
            # (B, 772),
            (B, D3),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)

        tensors = [a, b, c]

        total_cols: int = int(a.shape[1] + b.shape[1] + c.shape[1])

        def torch_copy(
            tensors: List[torch.Tensor], is_inplace: bool = True
        ) -> torch.Tensor:
            f = torch.zeros([B, total_cols], dtype=dtype, device=torch.device("cuda"))
            col_idx = 0
            for t in tensors:
                temp = f[:, col_idx : col_idx + t.shape[1]]
                if is_inplace:
                    temp.copy_(t)
                else:
                    f[:, col_idx : col_idx + t.shape[1]] = t
                col_idx += t.shape[1]
            return f

        def torch_cat(tensors: List[torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
            return torch.cat(tensors, dim=1)

        ref = torch_cat(tensors)
        real = torch_copy(tensors, is_inplace=False)

        torch.testing.assert_allclose(ref, real)

        if provider == "pt_eager":
            fn = lambda: torch_cat(tensors)  # noqa E731
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        elif provider == "stack":

            def torch_stack(tensors: List[torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
                return torch.stack(tensors, dim=1).view(-1, total_cols)

            fn = lambda: torch_stack(tensors)
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        elif provider == "copy":
            fn = lambda: torch_copy(tensors)
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported provider: {provider}")

    df = bench_cat.run(print_data=True, return_df=return_result)

    if return_result:
        return configs, df

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

messages.claude:
perf: split vectorized_elementwise_kernel to reduce libtorch_cuda.so binary size

Split the vec_size=8 path from the vec_size=[2,4] paths into separate
kernel instantiations. vec8 is exclusively used on sm_90 and sm_100, so
guarding it behind __CUDA_ARCH__ == 900 || __CUDA_ARCH__ == 100 lets the
compiler prune the vec8 specialization for all other architectures,
avoiding redundant template instantiations that bloat libtorch_cuda.so.

Also gate vec8 selection at launch time in launch_vectorized_kernel:
when the device's compute capability is not 90 or 100, clamp vec_size to
at most 4. This prevents dispatching to the (now sm_90/sm_100-only) vec8
kernel on older GPUs.

The ROCm path is left untouched; it keeps a single kernel definition and
continues using calc_optimal_vec_size to pick the vector length.

* Currently most of the values are dynamically fetched from setuptools, eventually we can migrate all the statically defined values to pyproject.toml and they will be autopopulated in the setuptool arguments.
* This controls what additional metadata shows up on PyPi . Special URL Names are listed here for rendering on pypi: https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/well-known-project-urls/#well-known-labels

These also clearly shows us what fields will need to be migrated to pyproject.toml over time from setup.py per #152276. Static fields be fairly easy to migrate, the dynamically built ones like requirements are a bit more challenging.

Without this, `uv sync` complains:
```
error: No `project` table found in: `pytorch/pyproject.toml`
```

messages.kimi:
feat: Support custom ops with decomposition in ONNX custom_translation_table

This change enables custom operators to work with custom_translation_table by iterating over the ONNX registry directly instead of only torch.ops.aten and torch.ops.prims. Previously, custom ops defined in user libraries were not discoverable when building the decomposition table, causing them to be decomposed even when a custom translation was provided. By using registry.functions.values() to collect registered ops, we now properly preserve custom ops specified in custom_translation_table during ONNX export.
messages.claude:
[ONNX] Support custom op with its decomposition in custom translation table

Fixes #150367

Refactors get_onnx_implemented_overloads to iterate over registry.functions directly instead of scanning aten/prims namespaces, so custom ops registered through custom_translation_table are recognized as ONNX-supported and preserved from decomposition during export. Previously, only ATen and prim ops were collected, causing custom ops with decompositions to be decomposed even when a custom translation table was provided.

Adds test_custom_translation_table_supports_custom_op_with_its_decomp to verify that a custom op (mylib::foo) is mapped to its custom ONNX translation (Sub) when a custom_translation_table is provided, and decomposed (Add) when it is not.

```
We want to support multi kernel dispatch. Here's the gameplan:

- We want to introduce a new inductor config called multi_kernel_hints: List[int] = [64, 256, 4096] in torch/_inductor/config.py
- Currently we have MultiTemplateBuffer which only generates 20 choices for a given matmul. We want to extend MultiTemplateBuffer so that instead of a single make_kernel_render we want to have len(multi_kernel_hints) + 1 make_kernel_renders. To do this you'll need to do a couple of things:
	- You'll need to update get_min_choice with a hint_override kwarg
	- Instead of accessing self.choice_timings the property,  you'll want to turn it into a method where you can pass in the override
	- You'll need to update _choice_timings_fn to also take in the override
	- You'll need to update `get_timings`, `do_autotuning`, `get_inputs`, `benchmark_in_current_process`, `benchmark_in_sub_process `, `make_benchmark_fn`, `autotune` in torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py to also take in hint_override
	- You'll need to update PersistentCache.lookup to also take in hint_override and use it in its cache key and benchmarking. In particular you'll want to update cache[op][inputs][precision][choice_hash] to also take in the hint_override.
	- You'll need to update finalize_as_triton_caller so that it finalizes multiple callers, one for each hint.
	- You'll also need to update V.graph.sizevars.size_hints to take in hint_override in torch/_inductor/sizevars.py
- As you can see in speedup_by_fusion in torch/_inductor/scheduler.py, when doing fusion we check to see if fusion is faster than separate and finalize the kernel if so.  You'll want to update `multi_node.finalize_as_triton_caller(ms_fused_choice)` so that instead we do something like `multi_node.finalize_as_triton_callers(ms_fused_choices)` where we still use the hint to determine whether or not to fuse but use also calculate the multi_kernel_hints fusion nodes and pass that in
- You'll need to update codegen_template in torch/_inductor/codegen/simd.py to have multiple kernel dispatch similar to codegen_node_schedule
- You'll also need to update torch/_inductor/codegen/multi_kernel.py to support shape specialized dispatch. The basic idea is for every unique shape we will check to see which of the len(multi_kernel_hints) + 1 is best and cache it.
- You'll see that in `call_kernel` in torch/_inductor/select_algorithm.py  we do some arg extension by adding the grid size. The current multi kernel implementation doesn't have support for this, particularly in the `benchmark_sub_kernels` in torch/_inductor/codegen/multi_kernel.py. Make sure we do the proper bookkeeping so we can benchmark the kernels with the right varying grid sizes.
- Instead of using a heuristic such as closest hint value to find the best kernel you should just run a benchmark across all the kernels for a particular shape to pick one
```

Enable caching for auto_functionalized and auto_functionalized_v2 higher-order operators by setting cacheable=True in their constructors. messages.claude:
feat: mark auto_functionalized HOPs as cacheable

Mark the AutoFunctionalized and AutoFunctionalizedV2 higher-order ops as
cacheable by passing cacheable=True to their HigherOrderOperator base
constructor. Previously these HOPs were not cacheable, so compiled
graphs containing custom_op calls (e.g. mylib::sin_inplace) could not
be reused across runs via the inductor fx_graph_cache, forcing a
recompilation each time even when the graph was identical.

Why: custom user ops wrapped through auto_functionalize are
deterministic given the same op and arguments, so there is no semantic
reason to exclude them from the fx graph cache. Marking them cacheable
lets the inductor skip recompilation for repeated graphs that include
mutating custom ops, reducing compile overhead in workloads that rely
on torch.library.custom_op. Fixes #151188.

Test Plan:
- add test_auto_functionalized_caching in test/inductor/test_codecache.py
  that exercises both v1 and v2 variants of auto_functionalized,
  verifying fxgraph_cache_miss/hit and fxgraph_lookup_write_file
  counters across repeated calls and across different custom ops.

messages.kimi:
fix: Prevent libgomp.so.1 from being loaded twice in wheel builds

The change modifies `.ci/manywheel/build_common.sh` to preserve the SO number for `libgomp.so.1` during wheel packaging, similar to how XPU dependencies are handled. This prevents the library from being loaded twice, which would cause `omp_get_max_threads()` to return 1 instead of the actual number of available threads.

A new smoke test `check_gomp.py` is added to verify that OpenMP threads are correctly initialized after loading both `libgomp.so.1` and `libtorch_cpu.so`. The test is integrated into `.circleci/scripts/binary_linux_test.sh` to catch this issue in CI builds (excluding cpu-aarch64).

This fixes the issue reported in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/149422 where loading libgomp twice breaks OpenMP functionality.
messages.claude:
fix: preserve so number for libgomp.so.1 to prevent double loading and add smoke test

Keep libgomp.so.1 unpatched (retaining its so number) in the manywheel build, alongside the existing XPU exception. Without this, libgomp.so.1 gets renamed with a sha256 suffix and ends up being loaded twice — once from the wheel and once from the system path (e.g. /usr/lib64/libgomp.so.1 on AlmaLinux). The double load causes omp_get_max_threads() to report 1, breaking OpenMP parallelism in PyTorch CPU wheels.

Add a dedicated smoke test (check_gomp.py) that loads libgomp.so.1 followed by libtorch_cpu.so and asserts omp_get_max_threads() != 1, guarding against regressions of this issue (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/149422). The test is wired into binary_linux_test.sh for non-cpu-aarch64, non-xpu, non-rocm, non-libtorch builds.
messages.minimax:
fix: prevent double loading of libgomp.so.1 which breaks OpenMP

libgomp.so.1 was being renamed via SHA256 hashing during wheel build,
causing it to be loaded twice (once as libgomp.so.1 and once as the
hashed version). This resulted in omp_get_max_threads() returning 1
instead of the expected thread count, breaking OpenMP functionality.

Keep libgomp.so.1 so number intact during wheel building, similar to
XPU dependencies, and add a smoke test to detect double loading.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix grad_query stride handling in flex_attention backward

The grad_query tensor in sdpa_dense_backward and flex_attention_backward was using empty_like() which doesn't properly preserve stride information. This change uses new_empty() with explicit stride permutation in sdpa_dense_backward and empty_strided() with inferred dense strides in flex_attention_backward to ensure correct memory layout alignment with the input query tensor.
messages.minimax:
fix: preserve stride information in flex_attention_backward grad_query tensor

The backward pass for flex_attention was using empty_like() to allocate grad_query, which does not preserve the stride layout of the original query tensor. This caused incorrect stride information when computing gradients, leading to incorrect results.

The fix replaces empty_like() with explicit stride-aware tensor creation using new_empty() + _permute_strides() in the higher order op and empty_strided() + infer_dense_strides() in the inductor kernel, ensuring the gradient tensor matches the expected memory layout.
messages.claude:
fix: preserve query stride order in flex_attention backward grad_query allocation

Replace empty_like(query) with explicit stride-aware allocation in both the
higher-order op backward (sdpa_dense_backward) and the inductor kernel
(flex_attention_backward). The new allocation constructs grad_query with
explicitly inferred dense strides that match query.get_stride() via
_permute_strides / infer_dense_strides + empty_strided.

Why: empty_like preserves the query tensor's storage layout, which may be
non-contiguous (e.g. GQA-style views where query is a slice/repeat of a
smaller kv buffer, or stride-permuted inputs). When the backward kernel
writes grad_query assuming the logical [Bq, Hq, seq_len_q, qk_head_dim]
layout but empty_like hands back a buffer that inherits query's physical
strides, the resulting gradient ends up with mismatched stride order and
produces incorrect grads (or crashes in inductor codegen) for non-contiguous
query inputs. By explicitly allocating a strided buffer whose strides are
the dense inference of query.get_stride() and then permuting to match
query.stride(), the grad buffer is laid out correctly regardless of the
input tensor's memory format, aligning grad_query handling with the
existing grad_key path (which already uses new_empty + _permute_strides).

messages.kimi:
fix(c10d): Improve device handling in barrier() with proper fallbacks and warnings

Remove the TypeError for non-list device_ids and instead handle device
resolution gracefully. The barrier() function now:

1. Uses device_ids list directly when provided, taking the first device
2. Falls back to bound_device_id from init_process_group() if set
3. Uses CPU device when no accelerator is available
4. Falls back to current device with a warning when no explicit device
   is specified, preventing hangs from all processes defaulting to device 0

Also removes the now-unnecessary test_nccl_barrier_device_ids_function_argument
test since non-list device_ids is no longer an error condition.

Update docstring to clarify that only one device id is expected.
messages.claude:
fix(c10d): infer barrier device from accelerator/group instead of requiring list

Previously, `barrier(device_ids=...)` required a List[int] and raised
TypeError on any other type, forcing callers to always supply a device
list explicitly. When users omitted `device_ids`, the code fell back to
`_get_object_coll_device(group)`, which could resolve to device 0 when
no device was bound — causing hangs or every process creating a context
on device 0.

This change reworks device resolution in `barrier`:
- Use `torch._C._get_accelerator()` to detect the accelerator on the
  machine, falling back to CPU when none is present.
- When `device_ids` is a list, use only the first id (per the updated
  docstring "Only one id is expected").
- When no `device_ids` is given, prefer the device bound via
  `init_process_group(device_id=...)` (`group.bound_device_id`).
- Otherwise fall back to CPU if the accelerator or collective device is
  CPU; if still unresolved, use the current device and warn once that no
  device id was provided, since relying on the default device 0 is a
  common source of distributed hangs.

The old `test_nccl_barrier_device_ids_function_argument` test, which
asserted the TypeError for a non-list `device_ids`, is removed since
that strict type check no longer exists; `barrier` now accepts the
broader resolution path described above.

[ROCm] Add sliding window attention support via AOTriton 0.10b

This commit adds sliding window attention (SWA) support for AMD GPUs by upgrading to AOTriton 0.10b. Key changes:

- Change ROCM backend to pass `std::optional<int64_t>` window_size_left/right directly instead of converting to `int` with `value_or(-1)`, since AOTriton 0.10b's V3 API accepts optionals natively
- Add `calculate_swa` helper to compute SWA parameters for V3 API, with graceful fallback when using older AOTriton versions
- Update AOTriton cmake to 0.10b, adding support for gfx950/gfx1201 (official) and gfx1101/gfx1151/gfx1150/gfx1200 (experimental)

messages.claude:
[ROCm] Bump AOTriton to 0.10b

Notable new features/optimizations for SDPA operators on AMD systems from AOTriton 0.10b:

* Official support of gfx950/gfx1201
* Experimental support of gfx1101/gfx1151/gfx1150/gfx1200
* Reduce libaotriton.so binary size by over 80%.
  + Without this optimization the binary size of `libaotriton.so` could be
    over 100MiB due to 2x more supported architectures compared with 0.9b.
    Now it is only about 11MiB.
* Support sliding window attention (SWA) in
  `_flash_attention_forward/backward`. Should fix #154582

See https://github.com/ROCm/aotriton/releases/tag/0.10b for full details,
including Known Problems.

Notable changes to SDPA backend:

* `std::optional<int64_t>` `window_size_left/right` are directly passed to
  ROCM's SDPA backend, because the default value `-1` is meaningful to
  AOTriton's backend and bottom-right aligned causal mask is implemented with
  negative `window_size_left/right`
* Some code clean up around `USE_CK_FLASH_ATTENTION`

The bump requires matching adaptor changes in the HIP flash-attention frontend
(aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/hip/flash_attn/aot/mha_all_aot.hip) and in
the CUDA dispatcher (attention.cu, attention_backward.cu), which now gate the
`non_null_window_*` int coercion behind `#ifndef USE_ROCM` so the ROCm backend
can consume the `std::optional` values verbatim. A new `V3_API` macro selects
the AOTriton v3 `attn_fwd_params`/`attn_bwd_params` path used for SWA, while
older AOTriton 0.9.x falls back to the existing v2 API and emits a runtime
warning that SWA is unavailable. The version guard is also relaxed from
`AOTRITON_VERSION_MINOR != 9` to `< 9` so 0.10b compiles cleanly.

The cmake/External/aotriton.cmake update pins the new 0.10b commit, drops the
`get_target_gpus_from_pytorch` macro in favor of passing `PYTORCH_ROCM_ARCH`
directly via `-DAOTRITON_TARGET_ARCH` (replacing the old `TARGET_GPUS` +
`AOTRITON_COMPRESS_KERNEL` options), and refreshes the manylinux/rocm and
sha256 lists to add rocm7.0 while dropping rocm6.2.

test/test_transformers.py and torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py are
updated alongside the bump: gfx950/gfx1201 are now officially supported
flash/efficient-attention targets, while gfx1101/gfx1150/gfx1151/gfx1200 move
under the experimental env flag. The `grad_query` fudge factor on gfx90a is
bumped from 650.0 to 670.0 to accommodate the new backend's numerics.

messages.claude:
[ci][einops] Add dedicated CI flow for einops version compatibility testing

Add a new CI job and test infrastructure to run the einops test suite
across multiple einops versions (0.6.1, 0.7.0, 0.8.1) on every PR.

What:
- Add `test_einops()` to `.ci/pytorch/test.sh` that installs each einops
  version in turn and runs `test/run_test.py --einops`
- Wire the new `einops` config into `.github/workflows/pull.yml` for both
  push and pull workflows on a linux.2xlarge runner
- Add `--einops` flag to `test/run_test.py` to filter to
  `test/dynamo/test_einops`
- Add `test/dynamo/test_einops.py` covering torch.compile + einops for
  functions, layers, and lazy-state recompile behavior

Why:
einops interacts with torch.compile (Dynamo) and has historically
regressed due to changes on either side. Without dedicated coverage,
breakages only surface downstream when users upgrade. Running the suite
against pinned einops versions on every PR lets us catch regressions
at the boundary between PyTorch and einops early — including a known
incompatibility with einops 0.6.1 tracked in
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/157417, which is explicitly
skipped in `test_functions`. The `test_no_recompile_on_lazy_state`
case additionally guards against spurious recompiles triggered by
einops' lazy initialization, which would silently degrade performance.

1. What changed: A fix was added to `torch/_subclasses/fake_tensor.py` to check if `func` has a `tags` attribute before accessing it (`hasattr(func, "tags") and torch.Tag.inplace_view in func.tags` instead of just `torch.Tag.inplace_view in func.tags`)

3. Type: This is a fix - it's fixing a bug where accessing `func.tags` without checking if the attribute exists causes an error.

Based on the reference examples' pattern (concise summary with technical context), here's the commit message:

fix: Check if func has tags attribute before accessing in FakeTensor validation

Add hasattr check before accessing func.tags to prevent AttributeError when func doesn't have tags attribute. This fixes a crash when using FakeTensorMode with operations like flex_attention that don't have tags defined.
messages.claude:
fix: avoid AttributeError when func has no tags attribute in FakeTensor validation

What:
- Guard the `torch.Tag.inplace_view in func.tags` check in
  `torch/_subclasses/fake_tensor.py` with `hasattr(func, "tags")`.
- Add `test_no_tag_func` regression test in `test/test_fake_tensor.py`
  that exercises `flex_attention` (a functools.partial-based attention
  op) under `FakeTensorMode(allow_non_fake_inputs=True)`.

Why:
Functions constructed via `functools.partial` (such as the
`flex_attention` score-mod wrapper) do not carry a `tags` attribute
like registered torch ops do. When `validate()` was called on a
non-Fake tensor input for such a function, accessing `func.tags`
raised `AttributeError` instead of the intended `AssertionError` about
metadata-mutating ops on non-Fake inputs. This broke tracing of flex
attention under fake mode with real (non-fake) inputs.

The fix falls back gracefully when `tags` is absent, treating the
function as not having the `inplace_view` tag, which matches the
prior behavior for any function that did not set that tag.

[inductor] sanitize triple-quoted docstrings in user triton kernel definitions

Fixes #155006

Inductor codegens triton kernel definitions into triple-quoted text blocks. When a user-defined triton kernel contains a triple-quote docstring (e.g., `"""doc"""` or `'''doc'''`), the codegen output becomes malformed and breaks compilation. This change escapes triple quotes in kernel docstrings and inline asm blocks during codegen to prevent syntax errors.
messages.claude:
fix: [inductor][user triton] sanitize triple-quoted docstrings in kernel definitions

Fixes #155006

When `triton.autotune_at_compile_time` is enabled, inductor codegens triton
kernel definitions into a triple-quoted text block. If the kernel source
itself contains triple-quotes (e.g. a user-defined triton kernel with a
docstring, or an inline-asm block carrying a `"""..."""` literal), the
embedded triple-quotes prematurely terminate the wrapping text block and
break codegen.

This change sanitizes such kernels before splicing them into the tuning
block:
- In `wrapper.py`, replace `'''` with `\'\'\'` so single-quoted triple
  quotes inside the kernel source no longer collide with the outer
  triple-quoted block emitted by the wrapper.
- In `graph.py`, replace `"""` with `\"\"\"` in the autotune defs string
  to handle the double-quoted variant symmetrically.

Add coverage in `test_triton_kernels.py` for both single- and
double-quoted variants of:
- `kernel_with_docstring_*` — kernels carrying a triple-quoted docstring.
- `kernel_inline_asm_*` — kernels whose `tl.inline_asm_elementwise` asm
  argument contains triple-quoted strings (guarded with `skipIfRocm` /
  `skipIfXpu` since PTX inline asm is CUDA-only).

The new kernel fixtures live in `triton_utils.py`. Each test compares
eager execution against `torch.compile(fn, fullgraph=True)` under the
`triton.autotune_at_compile_time` config to ensure the sanitized codegen
behaves identically to the original kernel.

Without this fix, user-defined triton kernels that legitimately include
docstrings or multi-line inline asm strings would crash at compile time
under autotune-at-compile-time, which is an otherwise valid and
increasingly common pattern.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix _foreach_copy indexing for large tensors

Fixes #156261

The `chunk_size` parameter in `CopyFunctor` was incorrectly typed as `int` instead of `int64_t`, causing integer overflow when processing tensors larger than 2^31 elements. This led to incorrect indexing and potential crashes when copying large tensors using the foreach_copy operation.

Changes:
- Changed `chunk_size` parameter type from `int` to `int64_t` in `CopyFunctor::operator()`
- Removed unused `opmath_t` typedef and used `scalar_t` directly in the copy operation
- Added test case with a 2^31+1 element tensor to verify the fix

The test case intentionally only runs once per dtype combination due to the high memory cost of allocating such large tensors.
messages.claude:
fix: _foreach_copy indexing for large tensors

Fixes #156261

The _foreach_copy CUDA kernel used a 32-bit int for chunk_size, which
overflows when a tensor contains more than 2^31 elements, causing
incorrect indexing. Switch chunk_size to int64_t in CopyFunctor so the
block-to-tensor offset math stays correct for very large inputs.

Also drop the opmath_t indirection in foreach_tensor_copy_list_kernel_cuda_
and dispatch Copy<scalar_t, scalar_t> directly. opmath_t promotes
half/bfloat16 to float, which is unnecessary for a plain copy and could
silently change the dtype semantics; using the real scalar_t preserves
the source type through the copy path.

The test adds a 2^31+1 element tensor to verify the fix (guarded by a
flag so it runs only once per dtype, since it is expensive).
messages.minimax:
Fix #156261 _foreach_copy indexing with large tensors

The bug occurred because `chunk_size` was `int` instead of `int64_t`, causing integer overflow when processing tensors with more than 2^31 elements. Additionally, using `opmath_t` instead of `scalar_t` in the Copy functor caused type mismatch.

This change:
- Promotes `chunk_size` to `int64_t` in CopyFunctor to handle large tensor sizes
- Uses `scalar_t` instead of `opmath_t` for the Copy functor to match the actual tensor dtype
- Adds a test case with a 2^31+1 element tensor to catch this regression

reroute index to fast implementation for indexing on 0th dimension (#151753)

Per title, improve x[index] cuda perf for the common case of indexing along the first dim, using vectorized gather kernel

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/151753
Approved by: https://github.com/eqy

Reland fast gather and index implementation (#151917)

This PR reapplies #151490 and #151753 together, and adds some missing checks when applying the fast path.
Previously missed checks:
1) indexing path has the stride in the indexed dimension in bytes, gather path has the stride in the indexed dimension in elements. When checking if fast path is applicable, I didn't take this difference into account, and still multiplied the indexing stride by element size. Fixed and test added
2) We want to take fast path only when we are copying contiguous equally spaced slices of inputs + all the necessary alignment requirements. The effective tensor size should be 2d (after all possible flattening is applied), the index stride in the last dimension should be 0, and, since in the kernel we are not applying non-indexing-related offsets to src tensor, the src tensor stride in the second dimension should be 0. This automatically happens for gather with dim=0, so I didn't put in an explicit condition for this. Sometimes all conditions except first dim "effective" stride equal to 0 are satisfied for scatter on non-zero dim, when index size in the indexing dimension is 1 and thus it is collapsed (dimensions of size 1 are always collapsed), e.g.
```
        # test gather along 1st dim that can accidentally trigger fast path
        # because due to index dimension in the gather dim being 1
        # an unexpected squashing in tensorIterator happens
        src = make_tensor((16, 2, 16), device=device, dtype=dtype)
        ind = torch.randint(2, (16, 1), device=device).view(16, 1, 1).expand(16, 1, 16)
        res = torch.gather(src, dim=1, index=ind)
        if res.device.type == "cuda":
            ref_cpu = torch.gather(src.cpu(), dim=1, index=ind.cpu())
            self.assertEqual(res.cpu(), ref_cpu, atol=0, rtol=0)
```
Note that if index size here was (16, 2, 16) instead of (16, 1, 16) then the middle dimension could not be collapsed and we wouldn't end up incorrectly taking fast path.
We could update the kernel to take this stride into account when computing offsets into src tensor, or we could specifically disallow non-zero stride on the first dimension. I took the second path for now.

[aten] 8 bytes aligned vector loads for bf16 and fp16 dtypes in torch.cat (#150233)

Enable aligned vector loading for 2 bytes datatypes in torch.cat. Specifically:
1. reduce the vector length to 8 bytes for 2-byte types (fp16, bf16 etc)
2. enable through a conditional template

The reason why 8-byte vector loading was chosen for fp16 and bf16:

```
# pyre-strict
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

import click
import pandas as pd

import torch

# @manual=//triton:triton
import triton

# CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICEs=7 buck2 run @mode/opt //scripts/zhaozhu:cat_bench

@click.command()
@click.option("--data-type", type=str, default="bf16")
@click.option("--return-result", type=bool, default=False)
def main(
    data_type: str,
    return_result: bool,
) -> Optional[Tuple[List[triton.testing.Benchmark], List[pd.DataFrame]]]:
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    if data_type == "fp32":
        dtype = torch.float32
    elif data_type == "fp16":
        dtype = torch.float16
    elif data_type == "bf16":
        dtype = torch.bfloat16
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported data type: {data_type}.")

    D1 = int(torch.randint(low=10000, high=50000, size=(1,)).item())
    D2 = int(torch.randint(low=100, high=1000, size=(1,)).item())
    D3 = int(torch.randint(low=500, high=1000, size=(1,)).item())

    configs: List[triton.testing.Benchmark] = [
        triton.testing.Benchmark(
            x_names=["B"],
            x_vals=[100, 1000, 10000, 20000],
            line_arg="provider",
            line_vals=["pt_eager", "copy"],
            line_names=["pt_eager", "copy"],
            styles=[("blue", "-"), ("green", "-"), ("red", "-")],
            ylabel="ms",
            plot_name=f"torch-cat-D1-{D1}-D2-{D2}-D3-{D3}-dtype-{dtype}",
            args={
                "D1": D1,
                "D2": D2,
                "D3": D3,
                "dtype": dtype,
            },
        )
    ]

    @triton.testing.perf_report(configs)
    def bench_cat(
        B: int,
        D1: int,
        D2: int,
        D3: int,
        dtype: torch.dtype,
        provider: str,
    ) -> float:
        warmup = 10
        rep = 3

        tensors = []

        a = torch.empty(
            # (B, 30108),
            (B, D1),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)
        b = torch.empty(
            # (B, 624),
            (B, D2),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)
        c = torch.empty(
            # (B, 772),
            (B, D3),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)

        tensors = [a, b, c]

        total_cols: int = int(a.shape[1] + b.shape[1] + c.shape[1])

        def torch_copy(
            tensors: List[torch.Tensor], is_inplace: bool = True
        ) -> torch.Tensor:
            f = torch.zeros([B, total_cols], dtype=dtype, device=torch.device("cuda"))
            col_idx = 0
            for t in tensors:
                temp = f[:, col_idx : col_idx + t.shape[1]]
                if is_inplace:
                    temp.copy_(t)
                else:
                    f[:, col_idx : col_idx + t.shape[1]] = t
                col_idx += t.shape[1]
            return f

        def torch_cat(tensors: List[torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
            return torch.cat(tensors, dim=1)

        ref = torch_cat(tensors)
        real = torch_copy(tensors, is_inplace=False)

        torch.testing.assert_allclose(ref, real)

        if provider == "pt_eager":
            fn = lambda: torch_cat(tensors)  # noqa E731
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        elif provider == "stack":

            def torch_stack(tensors: List[torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
                return torch.stack(tensors, dim=1).view(-1, total_cols)

            fn = lambda: torch_stack(tensors)
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        elif provider == "copy":
            fn = lambda: torch_copy(tensors)
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported provider: {provider}")

    df = bench_cat.run(print_data=True, return_df=return_result)

    if return_result:
        return configs, df

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

messages.claude:
fix: allow inf in scalar_tensor coercion for low-precision float dttypes

What:
In `aten/src/ATen/ScalarOps.cpp`, `fill_inplace` now uses a relaxed
cast path for Half, BFloat16, and the Float8_* types. Instead of going
through `value_scalar.to<scalar_t>()` (which throws on overflow), these
dtypes cast via `double` so that out-of-range values saturate to inf,
matching the behavior of the `torch.tensor` constructor.

Why:
`torch.tensor(1123581321.0, dtype=torch.float16)` returns `inf`, but
`torch.ops.aten.scalar_tensor.default(1123581321, dtype=torch.float16)`
raised `RuntimeError: value cannot be converted to type at::Half
without overflow`. This divergence crashed `torch.compile` programs
that materialize large pad/config scalars into low-precision tensors
under a fullgraph (see
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/158376#issuecomment-3079591367).
Aligning `scalar_tensor` with the constructor's relaxed float-cast
semantics eliminates the crash and makes eager/compiled behavior
consistent. Adds a minified dynamo test covering the regression.
messages.minimax:
fix: align aten.scalar_tensor overflow behavior with torch.tensor for float8/float16

Previously, torch.tensor(1123581321.0, dtype=torch.float16) produced inf while aten.scalar_tensor threw "value cannot be converted to type at::Half without overflow". This divergence caused torch.compile graphs to crash when float8/float16 scalar tensor operations encountered values requiring infinity representation. The fix applies a relaxed float cast for float8/float16 types, consistent with the torch.tensor constructor behavior.

messages.kimi:
[c10d][gloo] Fix allgather/gather/scatter for non-contiguous tensors

The newLikeFlat function was preserving strides from input tensors, which caused
issues when the input tensor uses non-contiguous memory formats like channels_last.
When performing collective operations, Gloo expects flat tensors to be contiguous,
but the preserved strides from channels_last tensors resulted in incorrect memory
layouts. Add preserve_strides parameter to newLikeFlat and set it to false for
Gloo operations to ensure flat tensors are always contiguous. Also add a test
case for allgather with channels_last memory format to prevent regression.
messages.claude:
feat: support non-contiguous tensors in c10d allgather/gather/scatter collectives

The previous newLikeFlat helper always called at::empty(sizes, t.options()),
which discards the source tensor's strides. For channels-last (and other
memory-dense but non-contiguous) inputs this produced a contiguous output
buffer that did not match the memory layout of the input, causing the
allgather/gather/scatter results to be laid out incorrectly and the
subsequent copy into the per-rank output tensors to corrupt data.

To fix this, newLikeFlat now accepts a preserve_strides flag (default true).
When the input tensor is non-contiguous and preserve_strides is true, it
builds the flat buffer with at::empty_strided using the input's strides so
the memory format is preserved across the collective.

The collective call sites in ProcessGroupGloo.cpp (AsyncAllgatherWork,
AsyncAllgatherCoalescedWork, AsyncGatherWork, AsyncScatterWork) explicitly
pass preserve_strides=false, because those paths flatten the output into a
single contiguous buffer for the underlying gloo call and must not inherit
the user tensor's strides. The default-true path keeps the existing
behavior for other callers.

Also adds test_allgather_noncontig in test_c10d_nccl.py, which runs an
all_gather on a channels-last tensor and asserts the gathered outputs
match the input, guarding against regressions for non-contiguous memory
formats.
messages.minimax:
fix: handle non-contiguous tensors correctly in c10d Gloo operations

When all_gather/gather/scatter operations in c10d Gloo receive non-contiguous
tensors (e.g., channels_last memory format), the previous implementation
preserved original strides when creating flat output tensors, which could
cause incorrect results since the actual data layout might not match the
preserved strides after collection.

This change introduces a `preserve_strides` parameter (defaulting to true for
backward compatibility) to `newLikeFlat` for tensor vectors. When set to
false, it takes a fast path using `at::empty()` instead of `at::empty_strided()`.
The Gloo ProcessGroup operations are updated to pass `preserve_strides=false`
when creating flat output/input tensors for async collective operations,
ensuring correctness for non-contiguous inputs while maintaining performance
for the common contiguous case.

A new test `test_allgather_noncontig` validates that all_gather works
correctly with channels_last tensors across multiple ranks.
