Update on "[RFC] Consolidate watchdog and monitoring thread"


This is the start of a series of efforts to consolidating auxiliary threads in PGNCCL, aka watchdog and heartbeat_monitoring threads. Right now we launch these two threads per PG instances, i.e., if users create hundred or thousand instances of PG or subPGs, we will end up with that twice many side threads which is not efficient. We have a RFC to consolidate them (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/146956). Right now both threads are assigned with so many functionalities so it is hard to do the consolidations in one shot, we will try to split it into at least two steps (PRs) to make it easier to test and review.

We did our first attemp in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/153668 but we also want to try to see if we can make monitoring thread a class. This PR is doing similar thing like https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/153668.

First of all, we start with the heartbeat monitoring thread which is relatively lightweight and conceptually easier to consolidate. What we did in this PR:
1. Make the heartbeat a singleton and make it static, instead of launching it per PGNCCL instance. We make all the logic or variables used in this thread either global or static so that it does not call instance specific API.
2. Remove the dependency on PGStatus which is PG instance specific. (We need to do more around PG Status if we want to consolidate watchdog thread later but it is out of the scope of this PR.)
3. Move the error propagation check to watchdog thread which is more relevant. This is totally fine since we rolled out EventCache out fully so watchdog hang is rare now.

Today there are two major functions inside heartbeat monitoring thread today: 
1. Check the heartbeat of watchdog thread every 8 minutes, we make the heartbeat of watchdog global instead of instance specific. If there are watchdog hang, it should be global. (I am open to better solutions to this one).
2. We check TCPStore every 30 sec to see if any watchdog timeout happens on other ranks, if so we will initiate a dump signal on the current rank as well. 

Previously we only let the thread on the default PG instance to do #2, now with this consolidation, we do FR dump signal every 30 secs and heartbeat check every 8 mins at the same time. If we break the polling loop early we will wait until the full heartbeat timeout (8 mins) before killing the whole program (when we first built heartbeat thread we want to directly kill the program when the watchdog or the whole program hang at CudaEvent destory or NCCL Abort).

   - Modified `ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp` to add validation that P2P tensors must be "non-overlapping and dense" even if they're non-contiguous

2. The Issue: The change adds proper validation for non-dense tensors in P2P (point-to-point) operations. Previously, P2P operations allowed non-contiguous tensors with just a warning, but they didn't check if the tensor was actually dense (non-overlapping). This could lead to incorrect behavior when sending/receiving sliced tensors that aren't dense.

3. Type: This is a fix - it's fixing a bug where non-dense tensors were not properly rejected in P2P operations.

Based on the reference examples showing similar patterns (fixing NCCL issues, explaining the problem and solution), here's the commit message:

fix: Validate non-dense tensors in NCCL P2P operations

Add validation to ensure tensors used in P2P (point-to-point) operations
are non-overlapping and dense. Previously, P2P operations only checked
for contiguity and issued a warning for non-contiguous tensors, but
did not properly reject non-dense tensors (e.g., sliced tensors with
non-contiguous strides). This could lead to incorrect data transfer
behavior. The fix adds an explicit check for `is_non_overlapping_and_dense()`
and throws a ValueError when the requirement is not met, matching the
behavior expected by the test suite.
messages.claude:
fix: validate P2P tensors are non-overlapping and dense in ProcessGroupNCCL

Previously, the check_gpu_single_tensor helper skipped all contiguity
requirements for P2P operations (send/recv), only emitting a warning when
a non-contiguous tensor was passed. This allowed non-dense tensors
(e.g., column slices that produce overlapping/strided memory) to be
handed to NCCL P2P calls, where the underlying memory layout is not safe
for direct transfer — leading to undefined behavior or silent data
corruption rather than an early, actionable error.

Add an explicit is_non_overlapping_and_dense() check on the P2P path:
transposed tensors (which remain dense) are still permitted, but
non-dense tensors now raise a ValueError with a clear message. Users
are still responsible for ensuring src/dst tensor shapes match.

Also add test_send_recv_non_dense_tensor to verify that both send and
recv reject non-dense slices on rank 0 and rank 1 respectively.
messages.minimax:
fix: enforce non-overlapping and dense tensor check for P2P operations

Previously, P2P operations (send/recv) only warned when encountering non-contiguous tensors but still proceeded, which could cause undefined behavior. This change adds proper validation to reject non-dense tensors (e.g., tensor slices) with a ValueError, since P2P operations require tensors to be non-overlapping and dense.

The test confirms that send/recv properly raise ValueError when used with non-dense tensor slices.

messages.claude:
test: improve async compile test stability and enforce strict zip semantics in sympy utils

Updated test_compile_subprocess.py to loop until two new compiled runs are observed
relative to the loop iteration's start, rather than waiting for a fixed total of four
runs. The previous assertion assumed exactly one background compile cycle, but the test
can legitimately trigger more than one (e.g. when the eager path triggers additional
recompilations), causing flaky assertEqual failures. Now we break out once a single
fresh background compile completes (compiled_runs delta of 2), and assert
stat_bg_started/finished == 2 with assertGreater for compiled_runs, matching the
actual async behavior.

Also fixed several zip() calls in test_sympy_utils.py and torch/utils/_sympy/functions.py
that paired mismatched-length sequences. Passing strict=False to these zips preserves
the prior lenient behavior explicitly, instead of relying on the default which is being
deprecated (PEP 618 / future strict-by-default direction). The zip in
TrueDiv.eval over sorted(sizes, strides) now also uses strict=False at both levels
to keep the unpacking semantics unchanged.

Finally set BitwiseFn.__qualname__ alongside __name__ when constructing bitwise
sympy functions. Without __qualname__ set, pickle serializes the synthetic class
under its original (non-renamed) qualified name, so unpickling fails to locate the
class. Added a pickle round-trip test for BitwiseFn_bitwise_and to cover this.

fix: Fix KeyError in resume block handling for nested graph breaks in Python 3.11+

This fixes a KeyError that occurred when handling resume blocks with nested graph breaks in Python 3.11+. The issue was that the block_target_offset_remap dictionary was keyed only by the resume offset, which could lead to collisions when the same resume function had multiple graph breaks at different initial offsets that resumed at the same instruction.

The fix changes the key from a single offset (int) to a tuple of (init_offset, resume_offset), ensuring that each unique graph break location gets its own remapping. This prevents the KeyError when Dynamo tries to look up block target offsets for nested context managers with graph breaks.

Additionally, this fixes a related issue where STORE_ATTR graph breaks didn't properly clear the exception table entry, which could cause incorrect exception handling behavior.

Test cases added:
- test_311_resume_block_keyerror: Tests nested graph breaks with torch.no_grad() in if/else branches
- test_311_resume_block_keyerror2: Tests doubly-nested torch.no_grad() with graph breaks
- test_store_attr_graph_break_key_error: Tests STORE_ATTR graph break handling

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/162313
Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/166176

fix(dynamo): fix block_target_offset_remap key collision across graph breaks

When a resume function has multiple graph breaks, the block_target_offset_remap was keyed only by resume_offset. This caused collisions when different graph break locations resumed on the same instruction. Now keyed by (init_offset, resume_offset) tuple.

Also fixes STORE_ATTR graph break exn_tab_entry handling and adds assertion for current_instruction.offset in create_call_resume_at.
messages.claude:
fix: [dynamo] resolve KeyError in resume execution block target offset remapping

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/162313 and
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/166176.

The resume execution cache keyed block_target_offset_remap by a single
resume offset (new_offset). This was incorrect when the same resume
function graph-broke in multiple places, or when graph breaks occurred
at different initial offsets but resumed on the same instruction —
the second graph break would look up a remap entry that didn't match
its block stack, producing a KeyError inside create_call_resume_at.

Root cause: generate_based_on_original_code_object mapped the resume
offset of the *current* graph break onto the original code object, but
the cache key only captured the resume offset, not the initial offset.
When two graph breaks shared a resume offset (e.g. nested context
managers with graph_break() inside, or if/else branches that both
graph-break inside a `with` block), the second lookup collided with
the first entry's block_target_offset_remap and failed to find the
expected setup_fn target offset.

Changes:
- Split the single `offset` parameter into `init_offset` (offset of
  the instruction currently being executed when the graph break
  triggered) and `resume_offset` (where to resume execution). The
  init_offset is needed because the same resume instruction can be
  reached from different graph-break sites, and each site needs its
  own block_target_offset_remap.
- Key block_target_offset_remap by (orig_init_offset, orig_resume_offset)
  instead of just the resume offset, so each distinct graph-break site
  gets its own remap table.
- Generalize find_new_offset into find_orig_offset(cur_offset) which
  returns -1 when the instruction is not present in the original code
  (this happens for instructions added in the prefix/prologue during
  nested graph breaks). init_offset is allowed to be missing; the
  resume_offset must always be found.
- Fix the remap_block_offsets matching: previously new_targets was
  built by filtering forward against targets, which could misalign
  block targets when the suffix had multiple candidates. Now match
  in reverse against reversed(targets) so post-prefix block targets
  align correctly between the resume code and the original code.
- In store_attr_graph_break, clear inst.exn_tab_entry on the copied
  STORE_ATTR instruction before emitting it to the output. The
  exception-table entry referenced a block that no longer exists in
  the resumed graph, which could trigger a KeyError when the resume
  machinery tried to remap block targets for that offset.
- Pass current_instruction.offset as init_offset from
  create_call_resume_at so the cache key reflects where the graph
  break actually occurred.

Tests:
- Move test_311_resume_block_keyerror into test_ctx_manager.py and
  add test_311_resume_block_keyerror2 (issue #166176) covering
  nested `with torch.no_grad()` + graph_break().
- Add test_store_attr_graph_break_key_error covering the
  STORE_ATTR graph-break path.
- Remove test_312_local_cell_overlap from test_repros.py; it was
  adjacent to the moved test but is no longer needed here.

[invoke_subgraph] Support pending unbacked symint (#149297)

The "PendingUnbackedSymbolNotFound" error is when an unbacked symbol is created within a piece of code, but this symbol never appears in any of the outputs. I believe the original intention is to help catch incorrectly written meta kernels, where users might've unintentionally created an unbacked symbol but never used it anywhere, but in our case this is intentional. An example is the following test case:

```python
    def test_pending_unbacked(self):
        class M(torch.nn.Module):
            @mark_compile_region
            def gn(self, x):
                u = x[0].item()
                return x * u

            def forward(self, x):
                for _ in range(4):
                    x = self.gn(x)
                return x

        torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True
        torch.compile(M())(torch.randn(8))
```

This fails with the error:
```
torch._dynamo.exc.InternalTorchDynamoError: PendingUnbackedSymbolNotFound: Pending unbacked symbols {zuf1} not in returned outputs (FakeTensor(..., size=(8,)),) .
```

In this case, creating the unbacked symbol is intentional, so we can bypass this using `fake_mode.shape_env.ignore_fresh_unbakced_symbols()`.

feat: Add config-based custom partitioning for CUDA graph ops

Replace the `register_should_partition_rule` API with a simpler config-based approach using `custom_should_partition_ops`. The new config accepts op names in "namespace::kernel_name" or "namespace::kernel_name.overload" format, making it easier for users to specify which custom ops should trigger graph partitioning without registering custom functions.

The previous `register_should_partition_rule` API required users to provide a callable with matching signatures, which was complex and error-prone. The new config-based approach is more declarative and integrates better with PyTorch's existing config system. The config changes are also properly handled in the caching system to avoid unnecessary recompilations when only the partitioning config changes.

What:
- Remove `_custom_should_partition_fns` WeakKeyDictionary and
  `register_should_partition_rule` from scheduler.py.
- Add `custom_should_partition_ops: list[str]` to config.py, accepting names
  in either op-overload-packet form (`mylib::baz`) or full overload form
  (`mylib::baz.default`).
- In `should_partition`, match the FallbackKernel's op name against the config
  list and partition unconditionally when matched (the previous callable-based
  rule is dropped; ops in the list always trigger a partition).
- Update test_cudagraph_trees.py to exercise both name forms and to verify that
  updating the config does not force a recompile (guarded by
  `fail_on_recompile`), while a cache miss after `run_and_get_code` recompiles
  with the new partition count.

Why:
- The callback API coupled partitioning decisions to user-supplied Python
  functions evaluated on FakeTensors at scheduling time, which is incompatible
  with config-driven recompilation semantics: changing the rule could not be
  expressed as a config change, so it neither triggered nor skipped recompiles
  in a predictable way. Moving to a config list makes partitioning rules part
  of the compile config, so Dynamo/Inductor's existing config-tracking and
  recompile-cache logic applies (the new test asserts `fail_on_recompile`
  holds when only the config changes, and that a forced recompile picks up the
  new partition count).
- Name-based matching (both overload-packet and overload forms) is simpler and
  avoids the need to hold OpOverload references via weakref, and aligns with
  how other inductor config options reference ops.
messages.minimax:
[inductor] replace register_should_partition_rule with config-based custom_should_partition_ops

The experimental register_should_partition_rule API is replaced with a simpler
config-based approach. Users can now specify ops that should trigger graph
partitioning by adding their names (e.g., "mylib::baz" for overload packet,
or "mylib::baz.default" for specific overload) to torch._inductor.config.custom_should_partition_ops
instead of registering a callback function. This removes the need for the
_custom_should_partition_fns WeakKeyDictionary and register_should_partition_rule function.

messages.kimi:
refactor: Remove unreachable deprecation warning function for TF32 precision API

The `warn_deprecated_fp32_precision_api()` function was defined but never actually executed because all call sites were placed after `return` statements. This dead code removal cleans up the unreachable warning logic that was intended to notify users about the new TF32 precision API but couldn't function as designed. The function and its 5 call sites in `allowTF32CuDNN()`, `setAllowTF32CuDNN()`, `allowTF32CuBLAS()`, `float32MatmulPrecision()`, and `setFloat32MatmulPrecision()` have been removed to improve code maintainability.
messages.claude:
[ATen] Remove deprecated TF32 precision warning API

What:
Remove the `warn_deprecated_fp32_precision_api()` helper and all its
call sites in `aten/src/ATen/Context.cpp`. The function previously
emitted a `TORCH_WARN_ONCE` directing users to the new
`torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision` /
`torch.backends.cudnn.conv.fp32_precision` API and warned that the
legacy `allow_tf32` / `allowTF32CuDNN()` / `allowTF32CuBLAS()` paths
would be deprecated after PyTorch 2.9.

Why:
The legacy TF32 control APIs (`allowTF32CuDNN`, `allowTF32CuBLAS`,
`setAllowTF32CuDNN`, `setFloat32MatmulPrecision`) already route through
the new fp32 precision backend internally, and the codebase has reached
the point where the new API is the supported path. The
`warn_deprecated_fp32_precision_api` warning was fired on every legacy
call (including read paths like `allowTF32CuDNN()` and
`float32MatmulPrecision()`), which produced noisy, repeated warnings in
workloads that legitimately still use the legacy accessors while
migrating. Removing the warning calls (and the now-unused helper)
eliminates that noise without changing runtime behavior, since the
underlying precision selection logic is untouched. This aligns with the
planned post-2.9 deprecation timeline referenced in the warning text and
keeps the migration path clean: the new `fp32_precision` settings remain
the recommended way to control TF32, while the legacy accessors continue
to work without spamming deprecation warnings.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add out_dtype support check for BMM Triton template selection

The Triton template for batch matrix multiplication (BMM) does not yet support the `out_dtype` parameter. Previously, the code would assert when `out_dtype` was specified with Triton templates enabled. This change adds a proper condition check to skip Triton template selection when `out_dtype` is specified and differs from the input dtype, allowing the fallback to `extern_kernels.bmm_dtype` instead. A test case is added to verify that max_autotune correctly falls back to the external kernel when `out_dtype` is used.
messages.minimax:
fix: handle out_dtype in bmm by falling back to extern_kernels when dtype differs

When bmm has out_dtype specified (e.g., float32 output from float16 inputs), the Triton template path was incorrectly selected under max_autotune, causing "NoValidChoicesError: No choices to select". This change modifies the Triton template selection logic to only use Triton when out_dtype is None or matches the input dtype, otherwise falling through to extern_kernels.bmm_dtype which properly handles out_dtype.
messages.claude:
fix: support out_dtype override in bmm inductor kernel

What
- Update `torch/_inductor/kernel/bmm.py` to skip the Triton template path when `out_dtype` is set and differs from the mat1 dtype, instead of asserting. This allows the existing `extern_kernels.bmm_dtype` fallback to handle the case.
- Add `test_bmm_out_dtype` in `test/inductor/test_max_autotune.py` to verify that under `max_autotune` with `max_autotune_gemm_backends="TRITON"`, the unsupported `out_dtype` combination raises an `InductorError` (NoValidChoicesError), and that in the non-autotune path the generated code uses `extern_kernels.bmm_dtype`.

Why
The previous implementation hard-asserted `out_dtype is None` whenever the Triton template was selected, which is overly strict: the Triton template simply does not (yet) support `out_dtype`, but a perfectly valid fallback (`bmm_dtype`) exists. The assert would crash compilation instead of gracefully degrading to the extern kernel path.

By gating the Triton template on `out_dtype is None or out_dtype == mat1.get_dtype()`, the unsupported case is excluded from the autotune choice set rather than triggering an assertion failure. This:
- Preserves correctness for cases the Triton template *can* handle (unchanged behavior).
- Routes the unsupported `out_dtype` case to the existing extern kernel fallback, which already supports dtype override via `bmm_dtype`.
- Aligns with the TODO already present in the code ("add out_dtype support for Triton Template"), deferring real Triton-side support rather than blocking the feature.

The test mirrors the documented contract: under TRITON-only autotune the bmm+out_dtype combo is intentionally unsupported and surfaces as `NoValidChoicesError`; without the autotune restriction the extern kernel path is selected.

messages.claude:
fix: break reference cycles in failed dynamo tracer output to prevent memory leaks

When dynamo tracing fails and triggers a restart or frame skip, the
DynamoTracerOutput attached to the exception retains references to the
failed output graph. This keeps alive a chain of objects (graph nodes,
FakeTensorMode, ShapeEnv, TrackedFake, FakeTensor) that would otherwise
be garbage-collected, causing memory growth across repeated failed
traces (notably observed on Python 3.14+).

Changes:
- Add `output_graph_for_cleanup` field to DynamoTracerOutput, populated
  even on the error path so the graph is still reachable for cleanup
- Add `_cleanup_output_graph()` that clears graph nodes and the
  ShapeEnv's tracked_fakes to break the
  FakeTensorMode → ShapeEnv → TrackedFake → FakeTensor cycle
- Call cleanup in both the restart-analysis and SkipFrame exception
  handlers in convert_frame.transform
- Add `Graph._clear_nodes()` helper in torch/fx/graph.py
- Remove Python 3.14 skip decorators from parametrization tests that
  are no longer failing once the leak is resolved; delete the
  corresponding dynamo expected-failure file

Update on "[RFC] Consolidate watchdog and monitoring thread"


This is the start of a series of efforts to consolidating auxiliary threads in PGNCCL, aka watchdog and heartbeat_monitoring threads. Right now we launch these two threads per PG instances, i.e., if users create hundred or thousand instances of PG or subPGs, we will end up with that twice many side threads which is not efficient. We have a RFC to consolidate them (https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/146956). Right now both threads are assigned with so many functionalities so it is hard to do the consolidations in one shot, we will try to split it into at least two steps (PRs) to make it easier to test and review.

We did our first attemp in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/153668 but we also want to try to see if we can make monitoring thread a class. This PR is doing similar thing like https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/153668.

First of all, we start with the heartbeat monitoring thread which is relatively lightweight and conceptually easier to consolidate. What we did in this PR:
1. Make the heartbeat a singleton and make it static, instead of launching it per PGNCCL instance. We make all the logic or variables used in this thread either global or static so that it does not call instance specific API.
2. Remove the dependency on PGStatus which is PG instance specific. (We need to do more around PG Status if we want to consolidate watchdog thread later but it is out of the scope of this PR.)
3. Move the error propagation check to watchdog thread which is more relevant. This is totally fine since we rolled out EventCache out fully so watchdog hang is rare now.

Today there are two major functions inside heartbeat monitoring thread today: 
1. Check the heartbeat of watchdog thread every 8 minutes, we make the heartbeat of watchdog global instead of instance specific. If there are watchdog hang, it should be global. (I am open to better solutions to this one).
2. We check TCPStore every 30 sec to see if any watchdog timeout happens on other ranks, if so we will initiate a dump signal on the current rank as well. 

Previously we only let the thread on the default PG instance to do #2, now with this consolidation, we do FR dump signal every 30 secs and heartbeat check every 8 mins at the same time. If we break the polling loop early we will wait until the full heartbeat timeout (8 mins) before killing the whole program (when we first built heartbeat thread we want to directly kill the program when the watchdog or the whole program hang at CudaEvent destory or NCCL Abort).

cc H-Huang awgu wanchaol fegin wz337 wconstab d4l3k

[c10d][fr] Add counters for FR dump and reduce its timeout to finish dump before watchdog timeout (#151329)

After https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/150652, we still see some ranks missing dumps. Upon looking further, the case is that FR dump timed out for its first attempt:
watchdog thread: notify FR dump -> wait for 1 mins -> throw watchdog timeout -> notify elastic to kill process
FR dump thread: received FR dump signal -> timeout after 1 mins with first attempt -> started 2nd attempt -> got killed.

So we want to make the FR dump timeout shorter, in reality, the log shows that the dump finished within one sec. Even if we consider a very slow speed like 200K/s the usual size FR (1MB at most) takes around 5 secs, so 15 secs is like 3 times buffer.

Also we still let watchdog sleep for 1 min so that we can wait enough time for two dump to timeout and the following check like GIL checker to execute.

Also, if we get stuck in getting GIL or cuda hang, 15 seconds should be enough to detect the hang.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix race condition in NCCL async error handling by adding thread-safe getAsyncError wrapper

The changes address a thread-safety issue where ncclCommGetAsyncError could be called concurrently by both the watchdog thread and main thread without synchronization. NCCL does not provide thread-safety guarantees for this API.

Key changes:
- Add getAsyncError() method to NCCLComm class that acquires mutex_ before calling ncclCommGetAsyncError
- Update C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT_BASE macro to use NCCLComm wrapper instead of raw ncclComm_t
- Replace macro-based timeout loops in waitReady() and abort() with explicit implementations that safely check async errors while holding the lock
- Fix incorrect comm argument in split() to use source instead of sourceComm

This prevents potential race conditions between watchdog and main threads when checking NCCL communication errors in non-blocking mode.
messages.minimax:
fix: add thread-safe getAsyncError wrapper to fix race in ncclCommGetAsyncError calls

The NCCL API's `ncclCommGetAsyncError` does not provide thread-safety guarantees. When both the watchdog thread and main thread call it concurrently on the same NCCL communicator, a race condition occurs.

This commit:
1. Adds a new `NCCLComm::getAsyncError()` method that acquires `mutex_` before calling `ncclCommGetAsyncError`, providing thread-safe access
2. Refactors `waitReady()` and `abort()` to use the new thread-safe wrapper instead of the `C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT*` macros which directly called `ncclCommGetAsyncError`
3. Updates `C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT_BASE` macro to use the new `getAsyncError()` wrapper instead of direct `ncclCommGetAsyncError` calls
4. Fixes a bug in `NCCLComm::split()` where the wrong variable (`sourceComm` instead of `source`) was passed to wait on the parent comm
5. Fixes `ProcessGroupNCCL::collective()` and `collectiveCoalesced()` to pass `ncclComm` instead of `comm` wrapper to `C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT`
messages.claude:
fix: Make ncclCommGetAsyncError thread-safe in NCCL wait/abort paths

Summary (What):
- Add a thread-safe wrapper `NCCLComm::getAsyncError()` that acquires `mutex_` before calling `ncclCommGetAsyncError`.
- Update `C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT` / `C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT_SLEEP` / `C10D_NCCL_CHECK_TIMEOUT_GROUPEND` macros to accept the `NCCLComm` wrapper and route async-error polling through `getAsyncError()` instead of calling the raw NCCL API directly.
- Inline the wait/abort logic in `NCCLComm::waitReady` and `NCCLComm::abort` to use the same mutex-protected polling, and fix `split()` to pass `source` (the wrapper) rather than the raw `ncclComm_t` handle.
- Update `ProcessGroupNCCL::collective` / `collectiveCoalesced` callers to pass `ncclComm` (the wrapper).

Reasons (Why):
- NCCL does not provide thread-safety guarantees for `ncclCommGetAsyncError`, but in PyTorch's PGNCCL both the main thread and the watchdog/heartbeat threads poll the same communicator's async error state concurrently. The previous macros invoked `ncclCommGetAsyncError(comm, &result)` on the bare `ncclComm_t` handle without any synchronization, creating a race between the watchdog and the issuing thread that could corrupt the polled `ncclResult_t` or trigger undefined behavior inside NCCL.
- This is part of the broader watchdog/monitoring-thread consolidation effort (see RFC #146956 and the related series in #153668/#11ec09fb91), where auxiliary threads are being consolidated and their interactions with the communicator are being tightened. As that work increases the number of threads touching the comm, the unsynchronized `ncclCommGetAsyncError` calls become a more pressing hazard.
- Routing all async-error reads through `NCCLComm::getAsyncError()` centralizes the locking so every caller (macros, `waitReady`, `abort`, `checkForNcclError`-adjacent paths) benefits from the same mutex acquisition, rather than relying on each callsite to remember to lock. The existing callers in `waitReady` and `abort` already hold `mutex_`, so the direct `ncclCommGetAsyncError` calls there are left as safe inlined fast paths with an explanatory comment.
- The `split()` fix corrects a latent bug surfaced by the macro signature change: it was passing the raw `sourceComm` handle where the macro now expects the `NCCLComm` wrapper, so `source` (the wrapper) is the correct argument.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add cuDNN version compatibility check for CUDA devices with SM < 7.5

Add runtime validation to prevent cuDNN 9.11+ from being used with older GPUs that have compute capability below SM 7.5. This check runs during cuDNN initialization and raises a clear RuntimeError with a link to the compatibility matrix if an incompatible configuration is detected.

This prevents confusing runtime errors and silent failures that occur when users attempt to use newer PyTorch builds with cuDNN 9.11+ on older hardware like V100 (SM 7.0), ensuring users get immediate feedback about the incompatibility with guidance on how to resolve it.
messages.claude:
fix: validate cuDNN version compatibility with CUDA device compute capability

Add an early compatibility check in cuDNN initialization that detects
when cuDNN version >= 91100 (9.1.1+) is used with devices whose compute
capability is below SM 7.5. In this case, a RuntimeError is raised with
a clear message pointing users to the PyTorch release compatibility matrix
to install an appropriate PyTorch build.

Rationale: cuDNN 9.1.1+ dropped support for pre-SM 7.5 devices. Without
this check, users running newer cuDNN on older GPUs (e.g. Maxwell, Pascal)
would hit opaque runtime errors or silently broken behavior. Failing fast
during initialization with an actionable error message helps users diagnose
the version mismatch and select a compatible PyTorch wheel, rather than
debugging downstream failures.

cuDNN version 9.11.00 and later require GPU compute capability >= 7.5. This change adds a runtime check during cuDNN initialization to detect when cuDNN is incompatible with available CUDA devices and raises a clear error message linking to the release compatibility matrix.

Prevents cryptic runtime failures when cuDNN 9.11+ is used with older GPUs (SM < 7.5) by failing early with an actionable error.

messages.kimi:
feat: Add Intel GPU support for persistent reduction configurations in Triton heuristics

Add platform-specific logic to `_persistent_reduction_configs` to handle Intel GPUs differently from CUDA. On Intel GPUs, we let the Triton cost model decide shared memory usage rather than forcing `num_warps=1` to disable it. This change calculates `x_block` based on the number of loads/stores and workgroup size, applying configurations from #168335 to optimize performance on Intel hardware while preserving existing CUDA behavior.
messages.claude:
feat: [inductor][triton_heuristics] Add non-CUDA path for persistent reduction configs

When CUDA is unavailable (e.g. on Intel XPU), the previous code unconditionally
set num_warps=1 to disable shared memory, which is a CUDA-specific tuning
knob. On non-CUDA backends this forced shared-memory-off behavior that did not
match the hardware, leaving performance on the table for reduction kernels.

Per #168335, add a separate configuration path for the non-CUDA case. Instead
of hard-coding num_warps, let the Triton cost model decide whether to use
shared memory by passing num_warps/min_num_warps/reduction_hint as None.
The x_block size is chosen based on numel heuristics and the number of
loads/stores (>= 5 picks x_block=1) to avoid oversubscribing registers on
memory-bound reductions.

The CUDA path is preserved unchanged.</arg_value> multiplayer

[inductor] Fix persistent reduction config for non-CUDA devices (#168335)

When `torch.cuda.is_available()` is False (e.g. Intel XPU), apply different block size configurations from #168335 instead of reusing CUDA's `num_warps = 1` heuristic. The cost model in Triton now decides whether to use shared memory for these devices. Also adjust `x_block` based on `loads_and_stores` count to improve performance for non-CUDA backends.

messages.claude:
fix: enforce float32 dtype for MPS SDPA 2-pass sums/maxs tensors

The 2-pass attention path on MPS allocated `sums` and `maxs` using
`q_.options()`, which inherited the query's dtype (e.g. bfloat16 or
float16). Accumulating reduction statistics in low-precision dtypes
causes numerical divergence versus the CPU reference, particularly for
GQA workloads with long key/value sequences.

Force both tensors to float32 via `.dtype(kFloat)` so the reduction
accumulates in full precision, matching the behavior of the CPU/CUDA
backends.

Also adds `test_sdpa_2pass` as a regression test for
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/174861, covering bfloat16,
float16, and float inputs with GQA enabled. The test helper
`_compare_tensors` now accepts a configurable tolerance to accommodate
bfloat16's wider error band.

messages.kimi:
fix: Correct A_B_offsets initialization in brgemm scratchpad setup

Summary: Change `reserve(1)` to `resize(1)` for `A_B_offsets` vector initialization in `GemmHelper` constructor. The `reserve` call only allocated capacity without changing the vector size, causing undefined behavior when accessing `A_B_offsets[0]` immediately after. Using `resize(1)` properly initializes the vector with one element, allowing safe assignment to the first index.

This fixes a bug where the A_B_offsets vector was accessed out of bounds after reserving but not actually allocating the element, which could lead to crashes or incorrect behavior during brgemm execution.
messages.claude:
fix: use resize instead of reserve for A_B_offsets in GemmHelper

Summary: In the brgemm scratchpad setup, A_B_offsets was reserved with
size 1 but not actually sized. reserve() only sets capacity without
creating any elements, so the subsequent `A_B_offsets[0] = ...` write
accesses an out-of-bounds element, resulting in undefined behavior
(works only by chance when capacity happens to be large enough).
Switching to resize(1) properly allocates one element before writing to
index 0, making the access well-defined.

Why: reserve() allocates capacity but leaves the vector's size at 0, so
indexing into the vector immediately after is invalid. This kind of
reserve-then-index pattern is a common C++ footgun that can cause memory
corruption or crashes under certain allocators/builds. Using resize()
ensures the element actually exists before assignment.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/153764

messages.claude:
fix: prevent recursion in Identity comparisons against numeric atoms

Add fast-path comparison operators (__ge__, __gt__, __le__, __lt__) to
the Identity wrapper in torch/utils/_sympy/functions.py. When both the
Identity's wrapped argument and the compared operand are numeric atoms
(is_Atom, is_number, is_comparable), compare them directly and return
a concrete SymPy boolean, bypassing the default symbolic comparison
path.

Why: SymPy's default relational evaluation for custom function
subclasses recurses through the symbolic comparator. For Identity
wrapping simple numeric atoms (e.g. Identity(sympify("-6"))), this
caused infinite recursion (Python's RecursionError) in expressions
like `Identity(sympify("-6")) >= 0` or `Max(0, Identity(sympify("-6")))`.
Max/Min rely on these comparisons to pick the dominant atom, so the
recursion also blocked constant folding for comparable numeric
identities. Compound (non-atomic) expressions intentionally fall
through to the default path to preserve symbolic semantics.

Tests in test/inductor/test_utils.py cover: integer comparison without
recursion, comparable-number behavior in Max, and rational comparison
without recursion.
messages.kimi:
fix: Fix Identity comparison recursion and enable numeric comparisons

Add _identity_atom_compare helper and comparison operators (__ge__, __gt__, 
__le__, __lt__) to Identity class to provide a fast path for comparing wrapped 
numeric atomics against other numeric atomics. This prevents infinite recursion 
when comparing Identity objects with numbers and enables proper behavior in 
Min/Max operations.

The fix ensures that Identity(sympify("0")) >= 0 and similar comparisons work 
correctly without triggering recursion errors, and that Identity objects 
wrapping comparable numbers can be used in Min/Max expressions.
messages.minimax:
fix: add fast path for Identity comparison operators to avoid recursion

Identity's comparison operators were falling back to SymPy's default symbolic comparison path, which could cause recursion issues when comparing wrapped numeric atomics. Added `_identity_atom_compare` as a fast path that directly compares numeric atoms (integers, rationals) without going through SymPy's symbolic machinery. This also improves performance for common numeric comparison cases.

messages.kimi:
fix: Add workaround for Metal compiler bug with fused (x / A) % B expressions

The Metal compiler produces incorrect results when optimizing fused (x / A) % B expressions for integral types. This causes incorrect reads from non-contiguous tensors in scaled dot product attention operations.

Add `safe_mod` function to c10/metal/utils.h that prevents the compiler from incorrectly optimizing the modulo operation by marking the dividend as volatile. Update MPSInductor codegen to use `safe_mod` when generating ModularIndexing with div=65536 and non-power-of-2 mod values.

Add regression tests in test_mps.py and test/inductor/test_mps_basic.py to verify the fix works correctly for both the metal shader and SDPA split QKV use case.
messages.claude:
fix: [MPSInductor] Work around Metal compiler bug in fused `(x / A) % B` expressions

Add `c10::metal::safe_mod` helper that forces the modulo operation through a `volatile`-qualified parameter, preventing the Metal compiler from folding `(x / 65536) % B` into an incorrect single expression for integral types. The bug specifically manifests when the divisor is a large power of two (65536) and the modulus is not a power of two, which is exactly the pattern emitted by the inductor for `ModularIndexing` during SDPA q/k/v split on non-contiguous tensors — producing wrong reads and corrupted attention output.

In `torch/_inductor/codegen/mps.py`, `_print_ModularIndexing` now detects this pattern (`div == 65536` and `mod` is not a power of two) and routes the codegen to `c10::metal::safe_mod` instead of the plain `%` operator.

Adds two regression tests:
- `test_mps.py::test_metal_compiler_bug_workaround` directly exercises the failing shader pattern (`(idx / 65536) % 6`) and asserts correctness.
- `test_mps_basic.py::test_sdpa_split_qkv` covers the end-to-end failure path (non-contiguous q/k/v split feeding `scaled_dot_product_attention`) that originally surfaced the bug.

Why: without this workaround, `torch.compile`-generated MPS kernels silently return incorrect results for SDPA on MPS, with no compiler error to flag the miscompilation.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/175481

GPUs (ROCm/HIP) by using AMDGCN assembly syntax. When torch.version.hip
is True, the operator now generates AMDGCN instructions (v_mov_b32,
v_add_f32, etc.) with "=v" constraints instead of PTX. Also fixes string
escaping for multi-line AMDGCN assembly in Triton code generation and

messages.minimax:
[HOP] Add AMDGPU/ROCm support for inline_asm_elementwise

This commit adds support for AMD GPUs (ROCm/HIP) to the inline_asm_elementwise higher-order operator. Key changes:

- ASM syntax: PTX instructions (e.g., `mov.f32`, `add.f32`) replaced with AMDGCN equivalents (e.g., `v_mov_b32`, `v_add_f32`)
- Constraints: PTX constraint letters (`=f`, `=r`, `=h`) replaced with AMDGCN vector register constraints (`=v`)
- Multi-line asm: AMDGCN uses real newlines between instructions instead of PTX's curly-brace syntax, requiring proper escaping through the Triton wrapper layers
- bf16/fp16 handling: AMDGCN has no "h" constraint for 16-bit registers; uses f32 arithmetic with explicit conversion instructions (`v_cvt_f16_f32`, `v_cvt_pk_bf16_f32`)
- gfx950 requirement: Native bf16 conversion instruction only available on gfx950+; tests skip on earlier AMD architectures

The test is removed from the CUDA-only skip list in `run_test.py` and now runs on both CUDA and ROCm targets.
messages.claude:
[inline_asm_elementwise] add AMDGPU/ROCm support via HIP code paths

What:
- Extend inline_asm_elementwise tests, Inductor codegen, and hop_db to
  support AMDGCN assembly alongside the existing PTX (NVIDIA) path.
- Add per-test-case `torch.version.hip` branches that swap PTX mnemonics
  (mov.f32, add.f32, fma.rn.f32, cvt.u16.u32, ...) and PTX constraints
  (=f, =r, =h, ...) for their AMDGCN equivalents (v_mov_b32, v_add_f32,
  v_fma_f32, v_bfe_u32, "=v", ...), since AMDGCN uses newline-separated
  instructions and 32-bit VGPRs only.
- Update `torch/_inductor/codegen/triton.py` to emit AMDGCN asm/constraints
  via `repr(...).replace("\\","\\\\")` so embedded newlines survive the two
  Python string layers (cached wrapper file + triple-quoted Triton source).
- Update `torch/_inductor/utils.py` to split multi-line `format_node()`
  output on ROCm so every line receives the comment prefix, preventing
  bare newlines from breaking the generated wrapper.
- Skip the `add_bf16_native` case on pre-gfx950 AMD parts (MI200/MI300/NAVI)
  via `evaluate_gfx_arch_within`, since the native bf16 conversion
  instruction is only available on gfx950+.
- Re-enable `higher_order_ops/test_inline_asm_elementwise` in run_test.py
  (previously skipped) now that the suite runs on ROCm.

Why:
- inline_asm_elementwise was effectively NVIDIA-only: PTX mnemonics,
  semicolon separators, and "h"/"f"/"r" constraints are not valid under
  AMDGCN, so the op and its tests could not run on ROCm.
- AMDGCN differences that needed explicit handling:
  * Instructions are newline-separated (PTX uses ';').
  * VGPRs are always 32-bit; there is no "h" (16-bit) constraint, so
    16-bit ops (fp16/bf16/upcast) must round-trip through f32 and use
    conversion instructions (v_cvt_f16_f32, v_cvt_pk_bf16_f32, v_bfe_u32).
  * Multi-instruction PTX sequences (e.g. exponent extraction via
    shr+and) collapse to single AMDGCN instructions (v_bfe_u32).
- Newline handling in the Inductor codegen is required because the asm
  string flows through two nested Python string layers; repr()+double
  backslash keeps the `\n` intact after both parses.
- The bf16 native-convert skip is needed because v_cvt_pk_bf16_f32 only
  exists on gfx950+, and running it on older MI/NAVI parts would fail.
- Re-enabling the test in run_test.py closes the coverage gap that
  existed while the op was NVIDIA-only.

[refactor] Restructure ROCm xfails to mirror main XFAIL_DICTS organization

The original `ROCM_XFAILS` had a flat structure that only handled `batch_invariance`, unlike the main `XFAIL_DICTS` which is organized by test type (eager_equivalence, determinism, batch_invariance, unary_numerical, binary_numerical). This refactor breaks `ROCM_XFAILS` into parallel `ROCM_*_XFAILS` dicts by test type and wraps them in `ROCM_XFAIL_DICTS`, making the ROCm section consistent with the main structure and easier to maintain.
messages.claude:
[test][inductor] Restructure ROCm xfail dictionaries and expand coverage

Splits the single ROCM_XFAILS dict into per-test-type dicts
(ROCM_EAGER_EQUIV_XFAILS, ROCM_DETERMINISM_XFAILS,
ROCM_BATCH_INVARIANCE_XFAILS, ROCM_UNARY_NUMERICAL_XFAILS,
ROCM_BINARY_NUMERICAL_XFAILS) collected under ROCM_XFAIL_DICTS, mirroring
the structure already used for the non-ROCm XFAIL_DICTS.

Why: Previously is_expected_failure looked up the generic XFAIL_DICTS for
every platform, then layered ROCm-specific entries on top via a separate
ROCM_XFAILS dict. This mixed the test-type semantics (eager_equivalence,
determinism, batch_invariance, unary_numerical, binary_numerical) into
one flat mapping, making it hard to tell which category a given ROCm
xfail belonged to and causing entries to be silently shared across test
types that did not intend them.

The rewrite routes ROCm builds through ROCM_XFAIL_DICTS directly, so
each test type owns its own xfail set, and is_expected_failure becomes a
single uniform lookup. The restructure also exposes several previously
missing or mis-bucketed xfail entries (e.g. sigmoid/sub/gelu/layer_norm
for eager_equivalence, log1p/rsqrt/sin/tan/tanh for unary_numerical,
nn.functional.linear for batch_invariance) that need to be tracked on
ROCm due to backend-specific numerical divergence from eager.

messages.kimi:
fix: Ensure hipBLASLt handle exists before CUDA graph capture on ROCm

On ROCm, hipBLASLt handles are lazily created per-(device, stream) and perform internal allocations during creation. These allocations are not permitted once CUDA stream capture is active, causing failures when capturing graphs with cublaslt backend enabled. Proactively initialize the handle for the capture stream before capture begins to prevent this issue.

This change only affects ROCm builds (USE_ROCM) when the preferred BLAS backend is set to Cublaslt.
messages.claude:
fix: ensure hipBLASLt handle exists before CUDA graph capture on ROCm

hipBLASLt handles are per-(device, stream) and lazily created via
hipblasLtCreate, which performs internal allocations. Once stream
capture is active on the capture stream, such allocations are not
allowed and would cause capture to fail.

When the preferred blas backend is cublaslt, eagerly request the
hipBLASLt handle for the intended capture stream in capture_begin so
that any handle creation happens before capture begins. This mirrors
the persistent workspace/handle handling for cublas/hipblas and the
hipblaslt workspace fix that addresses memory growth during graph
capture.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/156495

exemplars.message:
[CUDAGraph Trees] support memory allocation on side stream (#152472)

I tried `beginAllocateToPool` instead of `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentStreamToPool` and the error in #151199 does not happen any more.

However, this approach is unsafe for multithreading. When multiple run_eager happens concurrently, we expect memory allocation to different mem_pool. Since beginAllocateToPool does not check stream, these memory allocation may happen on the same mem_pool.

So, I use `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool` to direct all memory allocation on the same thread to a given mem_pool. In particular, `_cuda_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool` records the launching thread id, and during runtime checks if the current thread id matches the launching thread id.

Fixes #151199

messages.claude:
fix: handle stream pointer extraction for non-CudaStream stream types in dynamo

The previous implementation in `CudaStreamVariable.var_getattr` assumed `self.value` was always a `torch.cuda.Stream`, falling back to `stream_id` for other stream types (e.g. streams from `torch.accelerator.current_stream`). This was incorrect: the default stream for non-CudaStream types has `cuda_stream == stream_id == 0`, but for actual user-created streams the `stream_id` does not correspond to the underlying CUDA stream pointer, leading to wrong values being propagated through `torch.compile`.

Switch to a capability-based lookup using `hasattr`:
- If `self.value` exposes `cuda_stream`, use it directly.
- Otherwise, fall back to `native_handle` (available on `torch.Stream`), which correctly resolves the underlying stream pointer.

Also fix the return type annotation to be a string forward reference (`"VariableTracker"`) since `VariableTracker` is not imported at module scope, and add `test_stream_pointer_extraction_edge_cases` covering extraction from user streams, default stream, and the `torch.Stream` path to guard against regressions.

Previously, `CudaStreamVariable.var_getattr` assumed all stream values were

non-Stream objects. This caused incorrect pointer extraction when streams had

```
import torch
import time

def benchmark_sdpa(config, iterations=100):
    device = config.get("device", "cpu")
    batch = config["batch"]
    heads = config["heads"]
    q_len = config["q_len"]
    k_len = config["k_len"]
    head_dim = config["head_dim"]

    q = torch.randn(batch, heads, q_len, head_dim, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    k = torch.randn(batch, heads, k_len, head_dim, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    v = torch.randn(batch, heads, k_len, head_dim, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)

    for _ in range(5):
        _ = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
        if device == "mps":
            torch.mps.synchronize()

    total_time = 0.0
    for i in range(iterations):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        _ = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
        if device == "mps":
            torch.mps.synchronize()
        end = time.perf_counter()
        total_time += end - start

    avg_time = total_time / iterations
    print(f"[{config['name']}] Avg time per run: {avg_time * 1000:.3f} ms over {iterations} iterations")
    return avg_time

def main():
    device = "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu"
    print(f"Running benchmarks on device: {device}")

    benchmarks = [
        {
            "name": "Vector Fast - Small q_len & moderate k_len",
            "batch": 1,
            "heads": 8,
            "q_len": 1,      # small query sequence length triggers vector fast path
            "k_len": 256,    # moderate key length
            "head_dim": 64,
            "device": device,
        },
        {
            "name": "Vector 2-pass - Small q_len & long k_len",
            "batch": 1,
            "heads": 8,
            "q_len": 1,      # small query sequence length
            "k_len": 4096,   # long key length triggers the 2-pass variant
            "head_dim": 64,
            "device": device,
        },
        # {
        #     "name": "Full Attention - Moderate q_len/k_len",
        #     "batch": 1,
        #     "heads": 8,
        #     "q_len": 128,    # longer query sequence length
        #     "k_len": 8192,    # matching key length for full attention paths
        #     "head_dim": 64,
        #     "device": device,
        # },
        # {
        #     "name": "Full Attention - Longer q_len/k_len",
        #     "batch": 1,

        #     "q_len": 128,    # very long sequence length
        #     "k_len": 8192,
        #     "head_dim": 64,
        #     "device": device,
        # },
    ]

    iterations = 100
    for config in benchmarks:
        benchmark_sdpa(config, iterations=iterations)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

messages.kimi:
Based on the code changes, this is a fix for the MPS SDPA (Scaled Dot Product Attention) kernels to properly handle non-contiguous/permuted input tensors.

Looking at the changes:
1. The Metal kernels now accept batch stride parameters (`qkv_batch_strides_heads`) to correctly compute memory offsets for batched inputs
2. The kernel logic is updated to properly calculate `batch_idx` and `head_idx` from the thread position
3. The dispatch logic in `Attention.mm` is relaxed from requiring full contiguity to only requiring that the last dimension (head dim) has stride 1
4. A regression test is added for issue #181133

This fixes a bug where permuted inputs would produce incorrect results because the kernels weren't accounting for batch strides properly.

fix: [MPS] Fix SDPA vector kernels to handle non-contiguous/permuted inputs (#181133)

The SDPA vector kernels were assuming contiguous memory layout and only using head and sequence strides, causing incorrect results when inputs were permuted or had non-standard strides. This fixes the issue by:

1. Adding batch stride parameters (q_batch_stride, k_batch_stride, v_batch_stride) and num_heads to the Metal kernels via a new uint4 buffer
2. Updating kernel thread position calculations to properly derive batch_idx and head_idx from the combined batch-head index
3. Adjusting pointer offsets to account for batch strides when accessing Q, K, V tensors
4. Relaxing the input contiguity check in Attention.mm from requiring full contiguity to only requiring stride(-1) == 1 (head dimension contiguous), avoiding unnecessary copies for permuted inputs

Fixes #181133
messages.claude:
fix(mps): support permuted/non-contiguous strides in SDPA vector kernels

Fixes #181133

The MPS SDPA vector fast-path kernels assumed Q/K/V tensors followed a
specific (contiguous or head/seq-transposed) layout, forcing every
other input through `.contiguous()` and silently producing wrong
results when callers bypassed the contiguity check (or when the check
mislabeled a permuted tensor as usable).

What changed:
- Pass explicit per-axis batch/head/seq strides (qkv_batch_strides_heads,
  a uint4) into sdpa_vector and sdpa_vector_2pass_1 via new buffer(12)/
  buffer(14) arguments, instead of relying on the kernel inferring the
  batch offset from head_idx alone.
- Decompose tid.x into (batch_idx, head_idx) using num_heads so each
  threadgroup addresses the correct batch offset for Q, K, V, and the
  attention mask.
- Loosen the host-side contiguity gate from
  is_contiguous_or_head_seq_transposed to can_use_kernel_strides, which
  only requires stride(-1) == 1 (the only hard requirement for the
  kernels' linear head-dim loads), letting permuted layouts flow
  through directly.
- Add test_fast_vector_permuted_inputs_regression reproducing the
  (B, S, H, D).permute(0, 2, 1, 3) failure mode against CPU.
messages.minimax:
[MPS] Fix attention kernel for permuted/batch-strided inputs

Fixes https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/181133

The MPS SDPA kernels previously assumed batch dimensions were contiguous (stride[0] == stride[1] * stride[2]), which broke when inputs arrived with non-standard strides such as from `.permute(0, 2, 1, 3)`. This caused incorrect numerical results because batch offsets were not being applied.

This change:
- Adds `qkv_batch_strides_heads` buffer parameter to pass explicit batch strides for q, k, v tensors alongside num_heads
- Derives `batch_idx` and `head_idx` from the flattened `bh_idx` (batch-head index) in both `sdpa_vector` and `sdpa_vector_2pass_1` kernels
- Updates all pointer arithmetic to include the correct batch stride offset
- Simplifies the contiguous check in the host code to only require `stride(-1) == 1` since that is the only hard requirement of the kernel

Also adds a regression test using permuted inputs that reproduces the original failure.

CUDA 12.9 is explicitly excluded from Windows builds as it is Linux-only. messages.claude:
feat: Add CUDA 12.9 binary builds for Linux and linux-aarch64

Adds CUDA 12.9 to the binary build matrix for nightly builds, supporting
x86_64 and aarch64 Linux across Python 3.10-3.14 (and 3.14t). CUDA 12.9
is Linux-only; Windows builds exclude it via list_without(CUDA_ARCHES,
["12.9"]) in the libtorch and wheels matrix generators.

Includes:
- CUDA_ARCHES, CUDA_ARCHES_FULL_VERSION, CUDA_ARCHES_CUDNN_VERSION entries
- aarch64 arch entry and PYTORCH_EXTRA_INSTALL_REQUIREMENTS pinned deps
  (cuda-toolkit 12.9.1, cuda-bindings >=12.9.4,<13, cudnn 9.20.0.48,
  cusparselt 0.8.1, nccl 2.29.7, nvshmem 3.4.5)
- almalinux and manywheel docker image build matrix updates
- generated workflow jobs for manywheel (cuda + cuda-aarch64) and
  libtorch shared-with-deps-release extraction/upload

Reason: extends PyTorch binary coverage to CUDA 12.9, filling the gap
between 12.6 and 13.0 so users on CUDA 12.9 runtimes can install matching
wheels rather than falling back to 12.6 or jumping to 13.0. Windows is
excluded since 12.9 binaries are not produced for that platform.

messages.kimi:
ci: Include architecture in Windows libtorch package names to prevent upload conflicts

The Windows x86_64 and arm64 libtorch packages were sharing the same filename, causing them to overwrite each other in the upload bucket. This change adds an `--arch` parameter to the extraction script and includes the architecture in the build name for Windows ARM64 builds, ensuring distinct filenames for different architectures.

Specifically:
- `extract_libtorch_from_wheel.py`: Added `--arch` argument and updated `compute_zip_prefix()` to include "arm64" in the zip prefix for Windows ARM64 builds
- `generate_binary_build_matrix.py`: Added arch detection and includes arch in build name for Windows ARM64 libtorch extraction configs
- Updated workflow templates and generated workflows to pass the `--arch` parameter
messages.claude:
Disambiguate Windows x86_64 and arm64 libtorch package names in CI/CD

Add an `--arch` argument to the libtorch extraction script and thread it
through the binary build matrix and Windows workflow templates. For
Windows arm64 builds the package name now includes an `arm64-` tag
(e.g. `libtorch-arm64-cpu-shared-with-deps-release`), while x86_64
builds keep the existing name.

Why: The Windows x86_64 and arm64 libtorch extraction jobs both produced
artifacts named `libtorch-cpu-shared-with-deps-release`. Because the
generated arm64 nightly workflow reused the x86_64 build name, the two
packages collided in the upload bucket and in the artifact store,
causing one to overwrite the other. Tagging the build name and zip
prefix with the target architecture keeps the two packages distinct so
both architectures can be published and consumed independently.

Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/156668
